articles.title: BBC allegations cost Tory and Reform donor a peerage, defamation trial told
articles.summary:
Mohamed Amersi is suing over Panorama episode that made claims of his suspected involvement in corruption

A Conservative and Reform UK donor lost out on a knighthood and a peerage amid…

blocks.text: A Conservative and Reform UK donor lost out on a knighthood and a peerage amid claims of his involvement in corruption, the high court has heard at the start of his defamation case against the BBC.
An episode of Panorama in 2021 and a BBC article caused “very serious harm” to Mohamed Amersi, his barrister, Oliver Powell, said on Wednesday.

The programme and article alleged strong grounds for suspecting that during Amersi’s work for the Swedish telecoms company Telia he was involved in deals that he knew or should have known were corrupt or involved corrupt payments.
In an opening statement to the high court at the start of a seven-week defamation trial, Powell said the claims made by the BBC went to the heart of Amersi’s reputation and integrity.

The barrister read a witness statement from Amersi, who donated £25,000 to Reform UK last year and who previously donated hundreds of thousands of pounds to the Conservatives. The businessman claimed in the statement he had been forced by the publicity to step aside from what he described as his educational philanthropy.
Amersi said the “scandal cost me a knighthood and a peerage” and that he was debanked by Union Bancaire Privée of Switzerland.

The BBC, which is defending its content on the grounds of truth and public interest, claimed there was no evidence that Amersi suffered serious reputational harm either from its programme – Pandora Papers: Political Donors Exposed – or the article, which remains online.
In its skeleton defence, the BBC said “no corroborating documentary evidence to support Mr Amersi’s assertions has been disclosed” and suggested there were factual inaccuracies in his statement.

The focus of the BBC’s reporting in 2021 was Amersi’s work as an adviser to Telia, then known as TeliaSonera, in Uzbekistan along with a payment of $220m (£165m) made in January 2010 to a Gibraltar company called Takilant.

Powell told the court: “The BBC’s case is that the real beneficial owner of Takilant was actually Gulnara Karimova, the eldest daughter of the president of Uzbekistan. And it is their case that she is said to have had influence over the regulator of the Uzbek telecommunications sector.
“Mr Amersi will say that neither he nor Telia knew or suspected that Ms Karimova was the ultimate beneficial owner of Takilant and there was no basis for saying that he should have known.”

Powell said that the BBC was relying on admissions by Telia to the US Department of Justice in 2017 in a deferred prosecution agreement. The BBC was suggesting that this offered evidence that the $220m was a bribe, Powell said. He said that any such admissions were untested “hearsay” and the court should give them “little or no weight”.

Powell pointed to a legal review commissioned by Telia, which did interview Amersi, and was “unable to determine with any certainty that there was any legal or financial connection between Takilant and Gulnara Karimova”.
In its defence, the BBC has claimed that Telia “entered into a whole series of corrupt deals and payments for the benefit of its businesses in (variously) Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Nepal”.

Amersi claims that the BBC has failed to provide any evidence of his knowledge or involvement in corruption in any of those countries, claiming that his “work for Telia in Uzbekistan was very limited in scope during a very short period of fewer than six weeks in December 2009 and 2010”.
Amersi further claims there is “no contemporaneous (or other) evidence to suggest that [he] knew or should have known that Takilant was secretly owned (as the defendant claims) by Karimova”.
He has claimed that the BBC “seriously misled its readers and viewers by suggesting that [he] had been centrally involved in the payment of a ‘bribe’ to Karimova”.
The court heard from Amersi’s barrister that the BBC was offering “inference and generalised suspicion rather than any evidential foundation” in seeking to defend its reporting.

Amersi is seeking damages, “including aggravated damages”, and an injunction to prevent further publication of the statements he argues are defamatory. He will give evidence for six days from 11 November.
The case continues.

articles.title: The bottomless depths of Donald Trump’s midterm rally bigotry
articles.summary:
Both Obama and Trump are on the campaign trail, but only one of them appears to be descending into madness

  • This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland.…

blocks.text: Barack Obama versus Donald Trump. It is the presidential election that never happened but has come to define an era of US politics.

Obama is back on the campaign trail for the midterms, still electrifying crowds, earning shouts of “We love you!” and skewering his successor. “What’s up with the gold?” he asked a crowd in Detroit. “I mean, he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” This has, predictably, set off a mini culture war involving questions of elitism and the tastefulness of chain restaurants.

Trump’s election to the White House 10 years ago next month owed much to a racist backlash against America’s first Black president as white Christians shifted from majority to minority. He had pushed conspiracy theories about Obama’s birthplace and promised to build a border wall to keep out criminals and rapists.

Indeed, election campaigns are a furnace in which pretence burns away and essential character is exposed. They certainly bring out the worst in Trump. This year’s midterms effort, in which he is averaging about a rally a day and fighting bad polls like a cornered animal, is a case in point.

Has any president’s closing message ever been so Islamophobic, misogynistic and racist, not to mention downright deranged and bizarre? It is like watching a man vomit up bigotry that has been poisoning his soul for decades. Just when you think Trump has hit rock bottom, he produces a jackhammer and starts tunnelling to a new nadir of nastiness.

He still relishes calling Obama by his full name, Barack Hussein Obama, with an emphases on Hussein. Now he has Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim senator if elected, in his sights.

In Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, he called El-Sayed a “jihadist” who is “on the side of the terrorists” and would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate”. Trump repeatedly invoked the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers onboard United flight 93.

There is no evidence for any of this. But Trump is on an Islamophobic tear. He has repeatedly attacked Ilhan Omar, the Somali-born congresswoman of Minnesota, while his justice department banged on her door at 6am to investigate alleged fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. Omar has said she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong”.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump after rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: One of Trump’s standard punchlines now is the racist and false assertion that 98% of people from Somalia in the US don’t work for a living. “They don’t really have to work because they steal so much,” he told one rally. “They all have a Mercedes-Benz.”
He told his overwhelmingly white fanbase: “Can you believe, low IQ, and they live better than you do? I don’t know what’s going on. Maybe they’re not as low as we think.”

Another highly peculiar theme of Trump’s rally blitz has been his obsession with the male physique. He said of the Ohio senator Jon Husted: “I looked at his ass, and then I looked at his legs. I said, ‘His ass, shit, it’s like, it’s like a pile of muscle.’” He also claimed to have “fallen in love” with Tim Scott, the South Carolina senator.

The objectification is not limited to men. Back in Michigan, Trump turned his attention to the posterior of the rapper Nicki Minaj. “I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before: Nicki Minaj,” he said. “That’s hard to miss. Stand up! That’s hard to miss.”
after newsletter promotion

How is all of this resonating with Trump’s supporters? I called Sharon Anderson, who has been to 81 Trump rallies and was entirely untroubled by his comment. She said: “If a woman puts her ass out there for attention and somebody pays attention to it – Trump didn’t try to rape her – what’s the big deal?”

Anderson, 70, who is from Etowah, Tennessee, and went to her first Trump rally in 2015, dismisses the notion that he is getting worse. “I’ve been doing this for 11 years. He’s not changed a bit in my opinion. Now, a lot of what he says is reported and a lot of what he says isn’t reported.”

Does she have any concerns about the president’s mental health? “Absolutely not! Do you know anyone that could do what he does? He speaks an hour and a half to an hour and 45 minutes every rally. It’s almost supernatural in my opinion,” she said.

Yet Trump, who is 80, has started making strange guttural sounds, somewhere between a burp and a hiccup, in the middle of a sentence. And on Sunday he unleashed a 1,300-word rant on social media about his relationship with the comedian Bill Maher, branding him a “COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER” and telling him: “Bill: Don’t call anymore. It’s useless.”

Judging by the midterm polls that favour Democrats, Obama might have the upper hand in this latest struggle between the two men. As power slips inexorably from Trump’s grasp, as it must for all lame duck presidents, how much more desperate and extreme can he become? What new degradations await?

His rantings and ravings are a grim omen as he enters the Apocalypse Now phase of his presidency. Like Col Kurtz, he is a god to a fanatical but shrinking band of followers. Like Col Kurtz, he may be on a final descent into madness. Two more years? The horror, the horror.

articles.title: Evacuation from Oleshky: How are preparations going?
articles.summary: A lawyer with the Save Ukraine Foundation, Myroslava Kharchenko, told DW about what has been happening in Russian-occupied Oleshky since a temporary ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump took effect.

image.caption: The view of Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region Image: 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Since a ceasefire took effect in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region on October 27, preparations have been underway to evacuate residents trapped there.

Following Russia's occupation of the town in 2022 and the flooding caused by the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023, residents were cut off from the outside world. All access routes to Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River, had been mined. Former Oleshky residents who managed to escape and talked to DW described hunger, no access to medicine, and no electricity or water. About 2,000 people are still living in the town.

According to the Save Ukraine Foundation, it has rescued at least 300 civilians from Oleshky over the past six months. DW spoke with lawyer Myroslava Kharchenko, who works for the organization, about preparations for the upcoming evacuation.
DW: A ceasefire is already in effect in Oleshky. Do you know whether any evacuation efforts have begun?

Myroslava Kharchenko: No, we do not have that information yet. What we do know is that the ceasefire came into effect on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time, which is 4 a.m. in Russia. Mine-clearing operations on the road began at around 8 a.m. What is happening inside Oleshky itself, however, is entirely within the military's remit. Everyone involved in this operation has been asked to maintain strict confidentiality. Any careless remark or action could jeopardize the entire evacuation effort.

What I can see is that information is being actively collected through closed internal local chat groups. Registration lists and application forms are being shared, and people are filling them out themselves. Organizers are contacting those who previously requested evacuation to verify details such as their date of birth and current place of residence. They are also asking people to provide contact information for neighbors or relatives who may be nearby or in the same building, because communications are extremely unreliable.

The organizers are also collecting information about the health conditions of those planning to leave. Among them are people who are ill, have limited mobility, or are recovering from recent injuries, including blast and mine-related wounds. We therefore expect those organizing the evacuation to ensure that medical assistance is available for those who need it.
How exactly is the evacuation expected to take place? Will people be evacuated through Russian-controlled territory or via the Dnipro River? Have any routes already been agreed upon?

As far as we know, a river route would be extremely dangerous. We have not heard any confirmation that such an option has been approved. It therefore appears likely that the evacuation route will pass through the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and possibly through Russia before people are able to reach Ukraine. For security reasons, however, none of these details are being made public.
What do you know about the number of people expected to be evacuated?

We are actually very pleased that the evacuation is not expected to take place in a single day. That is important because we hope that those who manage to leave safely during the first stage will serve as an example for others.
People still trapped in Oleshky are extremely afraid. There have already been numerous provocations, and this is not the first attempt to establish such a route or humanitarian corridor.

As a result, there is a great deal of suspicion. Those concerns are based largely on uncertainty, and some people may choose not to leave during the initial phase of the evacuation. Overall, however, we estimate that around 500 people may eventually be evacuated.
Oleshky ceasefire comes into effect in Ukraine war
How would you assess the role of Melania Trump in making this evacuation possible?

We are immensely grateful to Melania Trump for drawing attention to the humanitarian catastrophe currently unfolding in Oleshky. What is taking place there is in fact genocide committed by the Russian Federation.

We are thankful for her efforts and hope they will help make this evacuation possible. We will be even more grateful once most people are safely removed from the combat zone and arrive in Ukrainian government-controlled territory.

blocks.caption: Myroslava Kharchenko from the Save Ukraine FoundationImage: DW Novosti

blocks.text: When could the physical evacuation of civilians begin?

I can't say how long it will take. What seems clear, however, is that time will be needed to clear mines from the roads leading into the city. We also understand that many streets inside Oleshky are mined, so additional work will be required to make routes within the city safe.
There is a hospital from which people need to be evacuated. Nearby is a morgue where bodies also need to be recovered.

I do not know whether that will be included as part of this humanitarian corridor, but it is undoubtedly important. The bodies need to be identified and the causes of death established. That process will also take time, regardless of how quickly the military is able to work.

It is difficult to make any predictions because, as you can see, everything is being conducted under strict secrecy. Statements from both the Russian and Ukrainian sides have been extremely cautious, and that is clearly justified under the circumstances.

articles.title: Bryan Adams takes aim at Lake Ontario name change in new song
articles.summary: Bryan Adams's new song Lake Ontario criticizes the debate over renaming the lake as a political distraction while affirming its enduring name and history. It follows 51st State, another patriotic…

image.caption: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams, pictured performing in Toronto on in 2017, released his new single Lake Ontario on Wednesday. The song takes aim at talk of renaming the Great Lake. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Bryan Adams's new song Lake Ontario criticizes the debate over renaming the lake as a political distraction while affirming its enduring name and history. It follows 51st State, another patriotic track opposing the idea of Canada joining the United States.
Canadian rocker's latest single follows a recent run of songs focused on Canada
Bryan Adams turns the dispute over Lake Ontario's name into a political jab in his new single, accusing an unnamed leader of using the issue to distract from other controversies.

Released Wednesday, Lake Ontario moves from the lake's geological and Indigenous history to pointed references to Iran and the Epstein files, before returning to the refrain that the lake will keep its name.

Adams never names Trump directly, instead describing "one dude" who breaks a period of calm among people living on the lake's shores. He dismisses the idea of changing its name as a "real dog and pony show" and suggests the renaming debate is a distraction.

The song's message has found an echo in another Canadian rock classic. At a Toronto show on Aug. 29, Blue Rodeo invited the crowd to sing the Lake Ontario line from its 1993 song Hasn't Hit Me Yet. Thousands joined in, turning the lyric into a moment of Canadian solidarity amid the name-change dispute.

items: 'That moment was glorious': How a Blue Rodeo hit became a rallying cry for Lake Ontario's name
Bryan Adams takes aim at Trump with protest song 51st State

blocks.text: Adams takes aim at the 51st state idea

The release adds to a recent run of songs in which Adams has taken a more overtly patriotic turn. On Canada Day, he put out 51st State, a response to Trump's repeated suggestions that Canada should become part of the United States. The song's title and lyrics reject that idea, placing national identity and Canadian sovereignty at the centre of the track.
The powerful rock anthem never mentions Trump by name either, but it's abundantly clear who the message is for.

"Let me give you some advice, mister — you might have too much on your plate," rasps Adams in the chorus of the rough-and-tumble track. "Go'n load us up with tariffs, but we'll never be the 51st state."

Lake Ontario makes its case less like a rallying cry than a wry argument. It opens with references to the lake's geological history, Indigenous care and the lake's history of European exploration and industrial use. The lyrics call it the "lake of shining waters" and say the name is not "an executive order."

In a statement on his website, Adams said, "Empires and regimes, dictators and kings, they all come and go. Lake Ontario is forever." He described the song as being for people on both sides of the lake who believe "the current madness will pass."

Lake Ontario is a bonus track on the digital edition of Adams's coming album, How's It Goin', which comes out Nov. 6. The album also includes 51st State, The Ballad of Terry Fox, The Battle of Lundy's Lane and Diesel and Dirt.

On Instagram, Bryan Adams posted the album cover for How's it Goin' with the list of tracks, including The Ballad of Terry Fox, 51st State and his new single, Lake Ontario. (bryanadams and badrecords/Instagram)
A musical love letter to Canada

Adams has described the album as a musical love letter to Canada. Its songs draw on Canadian people, places and history, with influences the release describes as Celtic folk and rock. The track list suggests a mix of historical subjects and contemporary politics, from Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope to the current dispute over the lake's name.

Born in Kingston, Ont., and raised primarily in Ottawa, Adams has never shied away from speaking his mind. He has been calling for an end to Canadian content rules ever since his 1991 hit (Everything I Do) I Do it for You was deemed by regulators to be not Canadian enough because he collaborated with non-Canadians. As recently as last year, he called the system "archaic" and "really stupid," arguing it only serves to prop up mediocre homegrown music.

items: Bryan Adams decries Ottawa online streaming rules

blocks.text: With Lake Ontario, Adams brings his longstanding focus on Canadian identity into the current political debate. The song's central message is simple: political figures and disputes may come and go, but the lake, he argues, should remain Lake Ontario.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.
With files from Kayla McLean

articles.title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
articles.summary: With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies are set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.

blocks.text: Israel's election result is messy - here's why

Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.

With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.
Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.
Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.
With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from soldiers and diplomats yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.

Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.
If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.
During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades.
"It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.
He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction.
"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Benjamin Netanyahu called for "a strong right-wing national government"

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Benjamin Netanyahu called for "a strong right-wing national government"

Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc.

"The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."
Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.
Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority".
"We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."

The leader of the left-wing Democrats party told its partners in Eisenkot's bloc on Wednesday that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," Yair Golan wrote on X.

The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - appear to be heading for record representation because of a strong turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

The chairman of the Joint List, which has talked of providing an electoral "safety net" for the Jewish opposition, said on Wednesday that it was "ready and prepared to pave the way to oust the Netanyahu government".
"Change runs through a Jewish-Arab partnership - a genuine and equal partnership. Nothing less, and nothing more," Yousef Jabareen wrote on X.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gadi Eisenkot said the Israeli public had "spoken in favour of change"

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Gadi Eisenkot said the Israeli public had "spoken in favour of change"

United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".
Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hardline, religious-nationalist trajectory.

Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.

articles.title: Drake Janice STFU copyright lawsuit withdrawn
articles.summary: Ten days after a copyright lawsuit was filed against Drake, alleging he stole the chorus of Janice STFU, the lawsuit has been voluntarily dismissed.

image.caption: Drake looks watches first half NBA basketball action between the Toronto Raptors and the Chicago Bulls in Toronto on Oct. 21. A producer who had filed a copyright lawsuit against Drake has now withdrawn the case. (Frank Gunn/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Ten days after a copyright lawsuit was filed against Drake, alleging he stole the chorus of Janice STFU, the lawsuit has been voluntarily dismissed.
Producer who claimed to have written song's hook withdrew case
It follows strenuous denials from Drake's legal team — who refuted the claim from Aviel (Avi) Hirschfield, a Grammy Award-winning hip-hop artist and producer who had worked with Drake in the past.
Court documents obtained by CBC News show Hirschfield and his legal team have now withdrawn their case, "in its entirety without prejudice."

Previously, on Oct. 16, Hirschfield claimed he was inspired to write the lyrics and melody use in Janice STFU while driving a loaned luxury Maybach to Seattle and listening to I Follow Rivers by Lykke Li, an artist Drake had sampled before.

Hirschfield then allegedly recorded a demo with his original vocals over an audio file produced by a duo known for their work with Drake, FnZ. He sent it to multiple people hoping it would get to Drake.

The now-dimissed lawsuit alleged Hirschfield heard the song Janice STFU much later and "was stunned to hear Drake perform word-for-word, note-for-note, the exact same chorus that he [Avi] had recorded and sent around to FnZ and other producers who work with Drake."
The Toronto rapper's team has always maintained these allegations were completely false.

items: Drake denies stealing Janice STFU chorus

blocks.text: Janice STFU debuted in May at No. 1 on both the Billboard Global 200 and the U.S. Billboard Hot 100. The Iceman track is Drake's 14th chart-topper and officially broke his tie with Michael Jackson for the most No. 1 hits by a male solo artist.
Drake even held a series of parties to apologize to people named Janice who had been hounded by the song.
Hirschfield was not given a co-writing credit and was denied a share of the song's revenues.

items: Is your name Janice? Drake would like to apologize for his song Janice STFU with a very exclusive party

blocks.text: Representatives for Drake said he has "no connection or knowledge" of Hirschfield, telling Billboard, "Let us be absolutely clear: These allegations are categorically, unequivocally and completely denied.
"There is not one iota of truth to these accusations, and we reject every attempt to portray these claims as established facts."
With files from Griffin Jaeger

articles.title: Three plead guilty in $9m romance fraud scam targeting elderly Americans
articles.summary:
Twin brothers, 22, from Ghana and a 53-year-old American woman targeted older adults in 25 US states, officials say

Three people have pleaded guilty in a $9m romance fraud scam that targeted…

blocks.text: Three people have pleaded guilty in a $9m romance fraud scam that targeted elderly Americans.
On Monday, the US attorney’s office in the northern district of Ohio announced that twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
Identified as Jamal Abubakari, Kamal Abubakari, both 22, and Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie, 53, of Kula, Hawaii, the trio targeted more than 130 victims in 25 states, as well as in Germany and Austria.

The Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie targeted older Americans on dating websites and social media platforms from July 2024 to April 2026, conspiring with others to “fake personas to establish close, personal relationships with the victims which were often romantic in nature”, according to the justice department.
The trio at times used “artificial intelligence-driven video platforms to engage victims under fictitious female personas”, the justice department said.

The victims, after being misled by false stories, would then wire money to bank accounts controlled by the conspiracy members, with portions of the funds also being distributed to co-conspirators in Ghana and elsewhere.

As part of their scheme, the trio said they allegedly needed the money for medical emergencies, investment opportunities or travel fees to visit the victims, according to court documents reviewed by outlets.

“Victims report that they are left with absolutely nothing to sustain their lives going forward after a lifetime of work and saving. In addition, individual victims are ashamed and deprived of the trust they once had in their fellow human beings,” prosecutors said in the documents.
In total, the victims lost more than $9m, the justice department said.

As part of their plea agreement, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit jewellry which investigators seized at the time of their arrests, including luxury timepieces, as well as high-end watches, rings, chains, medallions and earrings.
They face a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, with sentencing for the brothers scheduled for 9 February 2027 and 10 February 2027 for Opoku-Boachie.

Other co-conspirators are awaiting extradition from Ghana where seized assets estimated to be worth more than $3m include a Lamborghini, a Tesla Cybertruck, a Mercedes-Benz and a BMW, the justice department said.

articles.title: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence and has assets seized
articles.summary:
Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’

An Iranian court has handed the award-winning film director Jafar Panahi a…

blocks.text: An Iranian court has handed the award-winning film director Jafar Panahi a new prison sentence of five years and one month and ordered the seizure of all his assets.

The 66-year-old, who won the Palme d’Or at Cannes last year for It Was Just an Accident, was sentenced in absentia, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the Iranian news outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said.

The charges against Panahi remain unclear. He returned to Iran in March from an overseas trip to promote It Was Just an Accident, despite having been sentenced in absentia last year to a year in prison ‌for “propaganda activities against the system”.
A friend of the film-maker, an activist based in Europe, told the Associated Press that he had spoken with Panahi on Monday evening after the sentencing and the film-maker had not been detained.

Nili said Panahi currently faced three open legal cases, and had not been notified of the hearing date for the latest one. He only learned of the proceedings after his client’s bank accounts were frozen last week.

Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said the sentencing, and the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, could violate Iran’s constitution, unless the authorities establish a clear legal basis linking the property to an alleged offence.
Speaking to the Guardian while in the US earlier this year, Panahi warned that the current “cycle of violence” in Iran could continue.

“What I have been depicting in this film is when the cycle of violence continues, then it becomes very difficult to stop it,” Panahi said. “Unfortunately, because of the savagery that is being carried out by the state, the fear is that this cycle of violence will continue.”
after newsletter promotion
The latest sentence has raised concerns among fellow artists over the risks facing those who continue to work independently in Iran.

The Iranian actor Setareh Maleki, who was forced into exile after starring in Mohammad Rasoulof’s Oscar-nominated film The Seed of the Sacred Fig, told the Guardian: “One of the greatest fears of a dictatorship is losing control over the stories people tell. When those stories cross borders and reach the world, they become impossible to silence. Jafar Panahi has told his stories too, and his sentence proves once again just how deeply the Islamic Republic fears even the act of storytelling.”

Inside Iran, a film-maker currently shooting a film in secret expressed support for Panahi. “We all support him, who brings us great pride. He hasn’t remained silent and instead voices demands of the Iranian people,” said the film-maker, who did not want to give her name.

She said she believed Panahi’s latest sentence was linked to his calls for unity during the January protests and his support for diverse voices inside Iran, including supporters of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s former shah.

The Iranian-British actor Nazanin Boniadi also condemned the ruling, saying: “Jafar Panahi has spent decades turning censorship into cinematic resistance, bearing witness to the suffering and resilience of the Iranian people. His latest draconian prison sentence is yet another attempt to silence a courageous artist whose work exposes the realities of repression in Iran.”

In a recent report, the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that Iranian authorities are intensifying their crackdown on artists, writers, poets, musicians and other cultural figures, “pulling peaceful voices into the same coercive security and judicial apparatus used to suppress dissent across Iran”.

articles.title: ‘This isn’t supposed to happen’: giant-slaying Fleetwood revels in fairytale win
articles.summary:
Fishing town in disbelief the morning after their footballing minnows beat mighty Arsenal on penalties

On a wet and windy night on the north-west coast of England, a League Two side…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent

blocks.text: On a wet and windy night on the north-west coast of England, a League Two side sensationally knocked the Premier League champions out of the Carabao Cup. But this is not just a fairytale story of giant-slaying; Fleetwood Town and Arsenal have an unlikely history that stretches back long before Tuesday night’s game.
Arsenal played at their iconic Highbury stadium until 2006, and Fleetwood’s ground has the same title, being named after Highbury Avenue, the adjoining street.

Fleetwood also play in red shirts with white sleeves in the style of the classic Arsenal kit. Nobody is exactly sure why, but according to Ray Curtis, a barman in the town’s King’s Arms: “Fleetwood’s first ever kit, the home kit, was given to them by Arsenal.”
And in the 2000s, not long after Patrick Vieira captained Arsenal, Fleetwood boasted a namesake star: a Brazilian striker called Magno Vieira.

At the 5,300-capacity Highbury on Wednesday morning, the floodlights that Fleetwood had hired for the occasion were being packed away. “It’s back to reality, back to being a League Two team, that’s our normal,” said Zsofia Wright, the ticket office and retail manager.

On Tuesday, the excitement and anticipation started early. “We started getting what team had turned up, who’d flown in, and the whispers started, and it’s like, ‘oh, they’ve gone quite strong’,” Wright said.
“So we were all planning to just enjoy the occasion. And then obviously, we went 1-0 up and everyone was kind looking at each other, like this isn’t supposed to be happening.”
She said it was back to reality when Arsenal equalised except that “the clock kept on going and the score didn’t change”.

blocks.caption: Television equipment is removed from the Highbury stadium on Wednesday after a match between teams 84 places apart in the football pyramid. Photograph: Colin McPherson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Wright said everyone was on the pitch after the dramatic penalty shoutout that saw the Premier League champions and Champions League finalists ousted from the competition. The next stop for players, fans and management was the stadium bar.
“Just incredible,” Wright said. “We were here till about half one last night. It was brilliant, amazing.”

“The atmosphere was crazy,” said Chris Newman, 33, who was at the match with his son. He returned to the club shop on Wednesday to pick up two souvenir programmes. “Everything happened so quick,” he added. “I just didn’t expect it at all.”

The shop has done a roaring trade over the past 36 hours, with half-and-half Fleetwood and Arsenal scarves proving especially popular. One buyer with a London accent said. “I’m a Spurs fan, it’s brilliant.”

Wright said the town was abuzz the morning after: “Bars, pubs that are struggling, they were open till God knows what time yesterday. We just hope it can continue throughout the season, just hope that attendances start to pick up, and get consistency back again through the gates.”

blocks.caption: Sharon Brooks with her Arsenal-supporting son, Ryan, who said he was still pleased his local team won. Photograph: Colin McPherson/The Guardian

blocks.text: The club’s nicknames – The Cod Army, The Fishermen, The Cods and The Trawlermen – all derive from the Lancashire town’s fishing industry.

Sharon Brooks, who was visiting a fishmonger by the harbour, said: “We thought it’d be three, four or five nil, but they did so well to get a draw and then win on penalties, and five brilliant penalties. It’s nice for a town like Fleetwood, and [against the] Premier League winners last season, they just surprised you didn’t they?”
Her 12-year-old son, Ryan, who is an Arsenal fan, said: “Even though I wanted [Arsenal] to win it, I’m pleased for them.”
In the King’s Arms, everyone was eagerly awaiting Wednesday night’s draw, which will decide who Fleetwood play next.

blocks.caption: Donald Maclean in the King’s Arms in Fleetwood town centre. He said such a result ‘had never been heard of before’. Photograph: Colin McPherson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Donald Maclean, who missed the game because he was on duty at a nursing home, said: “I saw the goals this morning and I was delighted, over the moon, Imagine Fleetwood taking down the Gunners! Never been heard of before, so yes, we’re all delighted about it. Brilliant!”
The Cod Army’s victory has delighted fans partly because it was so unexpected – Fleetwood sit 84 places below Arsenal in the football league pyramid.

blocks.caption: Fleetwood Town’s club shop has been doing a roaring trade in half-and-half scarves. Photograph: Colin McPherson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Michael Houton said he had thought the result impossible “because Arsenal shouldn’t have got beaten should they? Not against Fleetwood”.

Paul Dagger was so pessimistic about his team’s chances that he staked £200 at half-time on Arsenal to win at odds of 10/7. “Gyökeres [of Arsenal] scored within five minutes of the start,” he said. “I thought, oh here we go, money’s coming in now. You live and learn.”
Fleetwood fans hope it will be the start of something bigger than just a victory for lovers of the game. “The town needs it,” Dagger said. “As you can see, it’s full of charity shops and vape shops.”
Gary Gill, a retired crane operator, said: “I am a Fleetwood fan and I think it’s fantastic for the town. It’s going to bring coin.
“If they play with the determination they did last night, any team that comes to play now is going to be frightened. And normally, that’s not the case, they think it’s an easy win.”

blocks.caption: Gary Gill said other teams would now be ‘frightened’ of coming to play Fleetwood. Photograph: Colin McPherson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Jim Buckley said: “It’s magic. We’re a Mickey Mouse town of 25,000 people, there’s no train station. I mean at the Emirates, they can fit three towns the size of this town in there.”
He was not far out – Arsenal’s stadium can hold 60,000 fans.
The drinkers in the King’s Arms said the travelling Arsenal fans had had a good day out despite the embarrasing defeat.
Dagger said: “Two pound twenty a pint in here, two pound fifty a pint over the way. They couldn’t believe it, they were going, facking ‘ell, it’s eight quid where we are.”

blocks.caption: Bethany Taylor, right, at the Shark Chippy near Fleetwood harbour. She said she was expecting defeat until she heard the roar of the crowd at the final whistle. Photograph: Colin McPherson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Back near the harbour, at the Shark Chippy, there was a lunchtime rush. Dishing up cod and chips, Bethany Taylor said she lived near the ground and could tell the final score from the roar of the crowd and the flares. “It was good, brilliant,” she added. “We weren’t expecting it.”
“It’s an incredible result isn’t it?” said her colleague Louisa Smith.
But do they think Fleetwood can lift the Carabao Cup? “It’d be a struggle, but hopefully they will,” Smith said. “We wish them luck.”

articles.title: Tory Brexit was ‘harder’ than promised in EU referendum, says Andy Burnham
articles.summary:
Prime minister warns cabinet not to express opinions about future relationship with Brussels before review of options

Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum.

In another series of announcements connected to his plan to seek closer links with the EU, Burnham told ministers at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the current deal was a bad one, before writing to frontbenchers setting out his hopes to address this.

Brexit was also the main subject of Burnham’s exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, with the prime minister saying the UK had been “paralysed” by the lack of a Conservative plan after the vote.
A Downing Street summary of the cabinet meeting put his comments about Brexit above even those concerning the budget, which the chancellor, John Healey, was to deliver soon afterwards.

“The prime minister opened by setting out how he would shortly write to cabinet on the UK’s relationship with the EU,” it said, adding: “He said the Brexit deal left by the last government had been bad for the UK and had led to a harder Brexit than had been promised at the referendum.”

blocks.caption: Home secretary Shabana Mahmood is among ministers said to be concerned about the implications of a revised Brexit deal. Photograph: James McCauley/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The letter to ministers made similar points, and ended with a warning from Burnham that they should not express opinions about the future shape of relations with the EU before a review of longer-term options.

“It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period,” he said. “It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.”

It follows reports that some ministers, including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the idea of a revised deal potentially bringing back the free movement of people to and from the EU, something Burnham has talked up as a possibility.

The letter set out Burnham’s two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will stay within Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement – a process that will formally kick off when the prime minister attends a European summit next month.
Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail.

“I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain,” he said in the letter. “It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration. It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.
after newsletter promotion

“We hope the summit will lead to some important, concrete steps. Beyond it, we will need to consider the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan. I will set out the next steps for this process around the summit.

“Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.”

Any fundamental changes in the relationship “would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament”, he wrote, adding: “This is government policy to which cabinet collective responsibility applies.”
Challenged by Badenoch at PMQs about his Brexit plans, Burnham reiterated his criticism of the current deal, saying the UK “was paralysed by the party opposite” in the wake of the referendum.
In response, Badenoch said that Burnham had been using freedoms allowed under Brexit, for example, the ability to remove VAT from energy bills: “What he should be saying is: ‘Thank you.’”

articles.title: Healey gives households £100 to help navigate ‘global economic storms’
articles.summary: Payments to 20m homes part of package to cut energy bills and ease cost of living crisis, paid for by bank windfall tax

blocks.text: John Healey promised to steer Britain through “global economic storms” as he announced an energy giveaway of £100 to 80% of households in England, funded by a smaller than expected windfall tax on banks.
In his first budget, the chancellor said 20 million households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 payment – a measure he said would cost £2.6bn.

That includes equivalent funding for Scotland and Wales, whose governments can decide whether to replicate the measure. The policy will help a large number of middle earners, reaching houses worth up to about £600,000 in London.

“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said, announcing the payment.
The relief on bills comes at a cost to big banks via the banking surcharge rise, and to savers and landlords, who were hit with an unexpected tax rise.

Healey saidhis budget would shape Britain’s future on defence, energy, welfare and entrepreneurship. “This Labour government has set a course for fresh hope, good growth and support for those who need it.”
The chancellor also extended the VAT cut on electricity bills until next July, and as widely expected, cancelled fuel duty rises pencilled in by Rachel Reeves.

Healey said this would help businesses as well as consumers. “For millions of people, the cost of living and the cost of doing business are the same. The home is the office. The van is the family car,” he said.
He blamed the war in the Middle East for the deterioration in the economic outlook since Reeves’s spring statement, but insisted he would keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track.

“Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” he said, describing his statement as “a budget built on fiscal discipline, which matches immediate action today with clear direction for the future”.

He said higher inflation as a result of the Iran war was expected to cost the government £14bn more in interest costs and the Office for Budget Responsibility had downgraded its growth forecast to 1% for next year, from the 1.6% it expected in the spring.

Healey nevertheless promised to meet Labour’s first fiscal rule, on balancing current spending with tax receipts by 2029-30, but with diminished headroom of £15bn – against the £24bn that Reeves set aside in March. He said the cushion would be rebuilt to £22bn by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can.”
The chancellor said the energy package would be funded by a windfall tax on Britain’s banks and the unexpected two percentage-point income tax rise for landlords and savers.
He is doubling the additional levy the banks pay on their profits to 6% from the current 3% for 15 months from January. That fell short of the rise to 8% that many industry figures had expected.
after newsletter promotion

Healey lavished praise on the sector as he announced the measure. “I want to say directly to our banks: I celebrate and I am grateful for the role that you play,” he said. Bank share prices rose after the announcement, with NatWest and Standard Chartered up by more than 4%.

Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.
There was a package of policies that Healey said would tackle the “moral mission” of homelessness.
There will be no easing of fiscal drag, however, despite Andy Burnham previously expressing concern at the rate at which households were being pulled into higher rates of income tax.

Forecasts show that the freeze on tax thresholds will drag an extra 6.7m people into paying income tax and push 5.4m more into the higher rate band by 2031–32. The minimum wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 an hour, an increase of £910 to the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker.

Pensions will also rise thanks to the triple lock, but with new tax relief to keep pensioners from paying income tax as the state pension rises above the personal allowance for the first time. About 500,000 pensioners are to benefit.

Healey also announced sweeping new powers for regions, pledging all mayors would be given a share of income tax revenue from 2028. He said he intended that local and regional government would retain 100% of business rates income before the end of the decade.
He said the devolution package would be “new powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics”.

articles.title: Dolores Huerta, California labor leader and civil rights champion, dies aged 96
articles.summary: Huerta co-founded United Farm Workers union with Cesar Chavez, improving pay and conditions for farm workers

blocks.text: Dolores Huerta, an iconic 1960s labor union leader and civil rights activist, died on Wednesday in California at the age of 96, her family said.

Huerta was co-founder with Cesar Chavez, another veteran unionist and political activist, of the United Farm Workers union (UFW), which was credited with improving pay and conditions for agricultural workers through a series strikes, boycotts and protests in the 1960s and 1970s.

Huerta was born in New Mexico in 1930, and followed her father, a miner and farm worker, into union activism. As a political operative, she worked on the presidential campaigns of several Democratic party candidates, including helping Robert F Kennedy to secure the party’s 1968 nomination before he was assassinated, and aiding the elections of Barack Obama and Joe Biden.
“We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96,” her family said in a statement on social media.

“As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family. We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy.”

Huerta is credited with coining the phrase “Si, se puede!” (yes, we can), which became the slogan of the UFW, and which Obama adapted as a rallying cry for his successful 2008 campaign for the White House.
As well as serving as Chavez’s right hand at the UFW, the union said on its website, “she could also be the greatest thorn in his side.”

It said: “The two were infamous for their blow out arguments, an element that was a natural part of their working relationship. Dolores viewed this as a healthy and necessary part of the growth process of any worthwhile collaboration.”

It emerged only in interviews Huerta gave to the New York Times, published in March, one month before her 96th birthday, that their relationship was much darker than it was publicly portrayed. As allegations emerged that Chavez, who died in 1993, groomed and sexually abused a number of teenage girls, Huerta revealed that he had raped her during the winter of 1966 in a vehicle in a secluded California grape field.
Huerta, who was 36 at the time, told the Times she did not report the assault because of authorities’ hostility to the UFW, and a fear that nobody in the union would believe her.
Huerta was later engaged in a long-term domestic partnership and had four children with Chavez’s brother, Richard, who died in 2011.
after newsletter promotion
The UFW said Huerta was also “seemingly unaware of the tremendous impact she was having on not only farm worker women, but also young women everywhere” as a fierce advocate for women’s rights.
Four elementary schools in California, and one in Fort Worth, Texas, as well as a high school in Pueblo, Colorado, are named after her.
In 2012, she was among 13 people awarded the Presidential Medal of Honor, the highest civilian award in the US, by Obama in a ceremony at the White House.

articles.title: Canada not in a 'position right now' to agree to U.S. trade deal, Carney says
articles.summary: As trade talks intensify ahead of Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will only agree to a deal "when it suits Canadians."

blocks.text: Politics
As trade talks intensify ahead of Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will only agree to a deal "when it suits Canadians."
PM says government will agree to deal 'when it suits Canadians'
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 28, 2026 12:39 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Canada's not in a 'position right now' to agree to a U.S. trade deal, Prime Minister Mark Carney says.
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government is not yet in a position to agree to a trade deal with the United States, stressing that an agreement will only be possible "when it suits Canadians."
Speaking to reporters ahead of a Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday morning, Carney said Ottawa is looking for "the right deal for Canadians."
"We think there's deals that are in the best interests of Canada, first and foremost, but also are in the interests of the United States. That's always been the case. We've been consistent," he said.
"If those deals present themselves, we will pursue them. But we're not at that position right now."
As midterms approach, U.S. teases progress on Canada trade deal
With Canada-U.S. trade tensions emerging as a key issue ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, questions have swirled this week around whether a deal could be reached before the Nov. 3 vote.
U.S. President Donald Trump and other senior American officials have suggested in recent days that progress was being made.
"We'll have ​that settled pretty soon. They're willing to give us anything ​at this moment," Trump said during a rally in Michigan on Sunday.

items: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency
'I don't know' if Trump would honour a new trade deal: Carney

blocks.text: But while trade talks have intensified, sources told CBC News earlier this week that the conversations didn't mean an agreement was imminent.
A source familiar with the discussions told Radio-Canada that "key elements" of the discussions remain unresolved, adding, "We are not on the verge of an agreement just yet."
Canada-U.S. negotiations fell apart in August and Washington imposed steep tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. Ottawa announced its own "dollar for dollar" levies in response.
Carney was also asked on Monday about the prospects of a deal, saying that his government is ready "to sign an agreement that is in the interests of Canadians."

"We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August," he said. "To the extent to which the U.S. is moving towards accepting those aspects, then there's a greater prospect of a deal."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.
With files from Peter Zimonjic, Louis Blouin and Katie Simpson

articles.title: One year on, families seek justice after election violence
articles.summary: One year after Tanzania's deadly post-election violence, families are still seeking answers. A government inquiry recorded 518 deaths. DW research has documented apparent use of excessive force by…

image.caption: The evidence DW has reviewed indicates that police likely acted beyond the scope of their guidelines and trainingImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Warning: This article contains descriptions of violence.
For one family member in Mwanza, Tanzania's second-largest city, justice could begin with a simple act: an apology.
Raha, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, said her nephew, who she raised, was killed during protests that erupted following Tanzania's October 2025 general election.
"The government should have asked for forgiveness for what happened. Even just offering condolences," Raha said.
A year later, the family is still waiting for answers about the death of their loved one.
A disputed election, a deadly crackdown
The violence followed an election campaign marked by the exclusion of the main opposition candidate.

Tundu Lissu, leader of the opposition Tanzanian Party for Democracy and Progress, commonly known as Chadema, had been arrested and charged with treason in April 2025 and his party barred from contesting the election.

blocks.caption: A polling station is set ablaze as clashes erupt in Dar es Salaam on October 29, 2025Image: AFP

blocks.text: On election day and in the days that followed, protesters called for political reforms and the resignation of Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

A government-appointed commission, chaired by retired Chief Justice Mohamed Chande Othman and commonly referred to as the Chande Commission, found that at least 518 people died from "unnatural causes," many from gunshot wounds, and over 2,000 people were injured.
Othman said the death toll could be higher because some families buried their loved ones without taking their bodies to morgues or reporting to the commission.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) also said the actual number of people killed could be higher.
"It's very clear that it's far more than the 518 people that were presented by the commission," said Oryem Nyeko, HRW's senior Africa researcher.
Police likely acted beyond their guidelines
DW analyzed dozens of videos, interviewed sources, reviewed police guidelines and advocacy research, and obtained a leaked police report.

We could not determine the exact location or publication date of every video, as some of the footage was released later due to internet blackouts or anonymously, for fear of reprisals. However, elements in the footage, our sources, public reports, and an internal police report give strong indications that these videos do reveal pieces of what happened in the days following the election.

The evidence DW has reviewed indicates that police likely acted beyond the scope of their guidelines and training. The material reviewed by DW included cases in which people were killed who were not protesting, where protesters were killed by head wounds, and where protesters were beaten or degraded by people in uniform.

The police's specialized Field Force Unit, identifiable in some footage by its red berets and riot-control equipment, helmets, shields and heavy weapons, appeared repeatedly in the material reviewed by DW.

Separately, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation organization, documented incidents in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's biggest city and commercial capital. In one, the uniformed people are beating civilians with sticks. In another, they are located close to where protesters were shot and killed.

DW also identified incidents in which people who were not protesting appear to have been killed. In Mwanza, videos showed the bodies of young men reportedly killed by people in police uniforms while watching television in a video hall. The case was also cited by Human Rights Watch and flagged by the Chande Commission for further investigation.
Who was responsible?

Tanzania's police guidelines restrict the use of firearms to circumstances where they are absolutely necessary. Yet investigations by DW and human rights organizations documented incidents involving protesters with apparent gunshot wounds to the head and upper body and non-protesters shot while trying to flee or while outside during a government-imposed curfew.
Security analyst Nicodemus Minde said the commission left crucial questions unanswered.
"The Commission did not really tell us who was responsible and why," he said.
The presence of a police unit at an incident does not establish who ordered an operation or whether senior officials authorized unlawful force.
The Tanzanian President has described the unrest as an attempt to overthrow the government.
Police violence reports emerge after Tanzania election row
DW confronted the Tanzanian government on the allegations of excessive force by police. The Tanzanian Ministry of Home Affairs declined to comment, saying it would interfere with the legal process.
DW also asked the Tanzanian police for comment. No response had been received by the time of publication.
The Chande Commission recommended further investigation but did not identify security bodies, individual officers or commanders who may have been responsible.
A second inquiry, chaired by retired Justice Shaban Ally Lila, began gathering evidence in August 2026 to further investigate. Its findings are still pending.
'There is no justice'
For the family members of those killed, the inquiries have yet to restore trust.
Zuri, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, said her brother and her son were killed in the post-election violence. She asked why the government had not visited affected families.
"We lost our children; we lost our brothers. Why hasn't the government taken any initiative to at least visit us?" Zuri asked.
"They behave as if nothing happened. Is this justice? There is no justice in Tanzania."
German lawmakers press Tanzania over rights concerns

articles.title: Socialist Hasan Piker is suing conservative counterpart for ‘violent racist’ portrayal
articles.summary:
The $72.5m suit alleges Scott Jennings falsely told listeners Piker had a ‘plan of returning our country to lynchings’

The prominent socialist political commentator and influencer Hasan…

blocks.text: The prominent socialist political commentator and influencer Hasan Piker is suing his conservative counterpart Scott Jennings for $72.5m over comments on a podcast that he said portrayed him as “a violent racist” who advocated the lynching of Black people.

Piker’s defamation lawsuit, filed on Tuesday in US district court for the District of Columbia, states that Jennings misrepresented his comments in a podcast and subsequent social media post in August.

“He falsely told his listeners that Mr Piker had a ‘plan of returning our country to lynchings’. And then he falsely told his social media followers that Mr Piker ‘says the USA should resume lynchings against black people’,” the document said.

Piker, a California-based popular streamer on the Twitch platform, said Jennings, a political commentator for CNN who hosts his own independent podcast, the Scott Jennings Show, deliberately twisted the remarks to make it appear they were his real opinions.

In truth, the lawsuit said, Piker “was plainly ridiculing” the extremist position of a commentator on an earlier Twitch broadcast who said “woke” district attorneys deserved blame for policies supposedly harming Black Americans.

The episode played out in August 2024, the lawsuit said, and centered on a “cropped, shortened, and rearranged” 42-second video that originally circulated on conservative social media accounts consisting of a mash-up of Piker’s comments on various subjects.

It included a clip of what the lawsuit said was a “sarcastic mocking” by Piker during his own broadcast of the position of one of the two Black commentators, but which it said was edited to remove crucial context and make it appear they were his own opinions.

According to the lawsuit, Piker, on his show, summarized what the commentator had said. “He said, ‘We need more Klansmen, okay? Can we go back to a better time when lynchings were happening? This is what I like as a Black man,’” the court document said.

But the “manipulated” video, which Jennings played on his podcast on 11 August, omitted the words “he said”, and other contextual clues, such as Piker’s clear ridicule of the commentator’s position, it said.
Jennings, the filing said, “added his own caption to the video, presented as a direct quotation from Mr Piker: ‘Let’s go back to a better time when lynchings were happening’.
“Mr Piker never said those words. The original broadcast does not contain that statement. Neither does the manipulated video that Mr Jennings chose to air.

“Mr Jennings converted a sarcastic question, expressly attributed to and directed toward someone else, into a patently false first-person statement of Mr Piker’s own supposed beliefs, and then relayed that false statement to his viewers.”

The lawsuit also said that Jennings was publicly known to be in the running to become Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary at the time, providing “an additional reason to attack a prominent left-wing commentator whom the President himself had criticized”.
Piker is demanding a jury trial, and seeking $27.5m in compensatory damages, and another $45m in punitive damages.

Jennings has not commented publicly on the lawsuit. In an 11 August post on X with a link to the video online on Wednesday, Jennings wrote, referring to Piker’s support for Michigan’s Democratic candidate for a US Senate seat:
“Abdul El-Sayed’s best pal and campaign partner says the USA should resume lynchings against black people.
“Listen for yourself and understand what the socialists have in store for the black community.”
The Guardian has contacted Jennings for comment.
