articles.title: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors? More of the same is expected, with some small positives predicted.
articles.summary: A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say. Some small positives may be possible…

image.caption: Arab commentators have celebrated the success of Israel's Arab parties as possible 'kingmakers' in the tight election, including the Joint List (pictured here) — even though most Israeli Jewish parties say they won't govern with them Image: Jamal Awad/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: As Israeli politicians begin to try to build a coalition government, after an election that saw no clear winner, response from politicians in surrounding Arab countries has been muted or non-existent.

This may be because, for the time being anyway, it remains unclear as to whether the new Israeli government will continue with "business as usual" under incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or whether a new government headed by Netanyahu's opponents will take what is expected to be a more moderate domestic course.

Whatever the eventual outcome, the consensus is that there is unlikely to be a huge change in Israel's foreign relations with neighboring countries like Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt, and, further afield, the Gulf states. Nor is it likely to produce very different policies toward Palestinians, which many Arab populations in the region feel strongly about.

blocks.caption: Netanyahu opponent Gadi Eisenkot (pictured), head of the Yashar party, appears to have achieved 16% of the vote. But he will need to build a coalition in order to govern Image: Shir Torem/REUTERS

blocks.text: Both Netanyahu and his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot "are two sides of the same coin," Egyptian politician Mostafa Bakry wrote on X after exit polls seemed to indicate an Eisenkot victory (something that's increasingly contested) and Israeli-Arab parties had displaced Netanyahu's far-right allies. "Arab joy at Netanyahu's near-failure to form the government does not mean that what is to come … differs greatly from his predecessor."

"An Eisenkot government would likely be politically fragile, limiting its room for maneuver," Beth Oppenheim, a policy fellow in the Middle East and North Africa program at the European Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in a commentary last week. "The biggest differences from the current government would be at home: It would halt the judicial overhaul, open a state commission of inquiry into October 7th and pass a conscription law."

However, Oppenheim explained, "when it comes to foreign policy, there would not be a fundamental transformation. Netanyahu's post-October 7th security doctrine — pre-empting threats, operating far beyond Israel's borders and holding 'buffer zones' in neighboring territories — has been embraced by nearly all Jewish Israeli parties."
Palestinian Territories: No two-state solution

One of the election campaign posters for Netanyahu's Likud party bore a stark message — "The right or Palestine" — the message being that if voters did not choose Netanyahu and his right-wing allies, his opponents would be too accommodating toward Israel's Arab-led political parties and would be open to the establishment of a Palestinian state.
But observers believe that message is exaggerated, and that the two-state solution is already dead.

"Support for Palestinian statehood has collapsed across most of the Jewish political spectrum, and permanent Israeli control over Palestinians has become normalized," Oppenheim pointed out. With the exception of one party, "all mainstream Jewish parties support, or at least acquiesce in, the settlement enterprise in some form and publicly oppose a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines."
In August this year, Eisenkot himself said that, "there is no Palestinian state, and no Palestinian state will be established under the government we form."

An Eisenkot-led government would, however, cooperate with more left-wing Israeli parties, which have previously supported a two-state solution. Any new coalition may also need the backing of Israel's Arab-led parties, who are currently thought to have increased their seats in parliament to around 19.

But as Mairav Zonszein, senior Israel analyst at the International Crisis Group, told the news agency Associated Press this week, "At best, [a new government] would be able to slow down the extremely crazy acceleration that we've seen in the last four years of every aspect of Israel's aggression in the occupied territories and inside Israel itself."

A less extreme government would tone down religious messaging, might be less demanding when it came to conditions on disarming Hamas in Gaza, and could potentially move forward with the next stage of the Gaza ceasefire, agreed to in late 2025, but barely implemented. It might also do more to contain settler violence in the West Bank.

blocks.caption: A 2025 survey found that around 82% of Israeli Jews support expelling Palestinains from Gaza (pictured) and around 56% believe Arab citizens of Israel should be expelled Image: Bashar Taleb/AFP

blocks.text: "That's because [settler extremism] is a phenomenon that doesn't enjoy the support of the majority of Israelis, damages Israel's international reputation, and suppressing it is feasible," Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Policy Council, explained on social media.

"[A new Israeli government] would keep expanding the settlements and Palestinian statehood would remain taboo," Oppenheim wrote. "Without a diplomatic track with the Palestinians, further flare-ups of violence in the West Bank and Gaza are inevitable, destabilizing the region — and normalization with Saudi Arabia will remain off the table."
Saudi Arabia: Could anti-Netanyahu bloc bring normalization?

After the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Hamas and Israel's ensuing military campaign, which has resulted in at least 70,000 Palestinians killed and Gaza devastated, Saudi Arabia's conditions for normalization with Israel have hardened.
The country, hugely influential in the Muslim world, has put out several statements saying there could be no path to normalizing relations with Israel without some progress on Palestinian statehood.

Last week, at a meeting of foreign ministers from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, the Saudis co-signed a communique in which the four countries said Israel was "the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond."

blocks.caption: Video still from a Houthi attack on a Saudi airport in October, 2026. The Saudi government has reportedly rejected Israeli offers of help to fight Yemen's Houthi militia Image: AFPTV/AFP

blocks.text: But there is some cooperation between the two countries behind the scenes. Analysts say that if a government less hardline than Netanyahu's gets into power in Israel, it will be easier for countries like Saudi Arabia — but also the United Arab Emirates, Jordan and Egypt, which all have varying levels of backchannel cooperation and contact with Israel — to admit to this kind of behind-the-scenes diplomacy.
Syria: Security agreement revived?

According to a study published last week by Syrian think tank, Etana, Israeli troops have come as far as 1,160 kilometers (721 miles) into Syria from the two countries' disputed border, occupied Syrian land as far as 400 kilometers from it and carried out 1,996 ground operations in southwest Syria between January and September this year.

Before elections this week there was no chance of any kind of withdrawal from Syria because it would have been seen as "defeat," Ksenia Svetlova, an associate fellow at Chatham House and a former member of the Israeli parliament, told online publication Syria in Transition this month. But if the anti-Netanyahu bloc gets into power, that could change, she suggested.

blocks.caption: Israeli troops have destroyed infrastructure and roads in places like Hamidiyah in Quneitra, near the Golan Heights, in SyriaImage: Ercin Erturk/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: "A security agreement with Syria will become more probable, as many potential stakeholders [in a new, more centrist Israeli government] have spoken favorably about it in the past," noted Svetlova, who is also director of the Tel Aviv-based Regional Organization for Peace, Economics and Security, which works on Israeli-Palestinian-Arab partnerships. "However I do expect that it will take time as this government will be constantly attacked by the extreme right."

For months this year, Israel and Syrian diplomats negotiated a security agreement under the US' stewardship. But it came to nothing in late 2026 after Israel apparently refused to withdraw back to boundary lines established under a 1974 disengagement agreement.
Lebanon: More diplomacy wanted
Observers and media commentators in Lebanon say the Lebanese government would prefer to have Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc in power.

Lebanon and Israel are continuing to negotiate an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, where the Israelis claim they have established a "buffer zone" to facilitate their fight against Lebanese militia group, Hezbollah. The Lebanese argue the Israelis have in fact invaded their country.

And when it comes to negotiations around disarming Hezbollah and withdrawing Israeli troops, there's a perception in Lebanese political circles that Eisenkot would be easier to deal with than Netanyahu and his extremist allies.

blocks.caption: The Israeli military has enormous damage in southern Lebanon. At one stage, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of giving in to the US when he stopped bombing BeirutImage: Zohra Bensemra/REUTERS

blocks.text: This is despite the fact that Eisenkot is widely seen as the inventor of the so-called "Dahiyeh Doctrine," a military strategy that calls for asymmetric warfare in areas like Beirut's southern suburbs, where Hezbollah is based, to pressure both militants and their civilian support base.
A similar strategy is thought to be being implemented in southern Lebanon now, where whole villages continue to be razed by the Israeli military, even as active fighting has subsided.

Lebanese commentators are also optimistic that Eisenkot, former commander of the Israeli army, would have something in common with their own president, Joseph Aoun, who used to head Lebanon's armed forces.

"When Netanyahu was ousted from power between 2021 and 2022 by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid [now members of the camp led by Eisenkot], we were able to negotiate and conclude the maritime agreement," a Lebanese official told Lebanese daily, L'Orient Today, referring to a 2022 deal to share offshore territory.

articles.title: ‘Can’t return home for Undas? Hear mass, pray’
articles.summary: Filipinos unable to return to their provinces on All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days due to high transportation costs can remember the departed by hearing mass and offering prayers, Manila…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Vendors prepare floral arrangements at the Dangwa market in Manila yesterday ahead of All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days.
Edd Gumban, File

MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos unable to return to their provinces on All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days due to high transportation costs can remember the departed by hearing mass and offering prayers, Manila Cathedral vice rector Fr. Vicente Gabriel Bautista said yesterday.

While travel costs could hinder people from going home on Undas, people can “go to parishes in their communities and celebrate mass and after the celebration of the Eucharist, they could pray together as a family and remember them,” Bautista said.
Some Filipinos are mulling canceling their trips to save money as fares have increased due to soaring fuel prices influenced by the Middle East conflict.
Philippine Ports Authority general manager Jay Santiago earlier said they expect passenger traffic at ports during the holiday break to be lower than last year.

Meanwhile, about 2,529 security screening officers of the Office for Transportation Security have had their vacation leaves canceled to ensure sufficient personnel and uninterrupted operations during Undas.– Rudy Santos

articles.summary: Several closed-circuit television cameras at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport are broken, the Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA) admitted yesterday.

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am

At a Senate public services committee hearing, MIAA assistant general manager Antonio Mendoza confirmed the claim of Frenchman Anthony Claude Boukhors, who had lost a luggage with three luxury watches worth P18 million, at the transport network vehicle service pick-up area at NAIA Terminal 1.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Several closed-circuit television cameras at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) are broken, the Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA) admitted yesterday.
Attending the hearing virtually from Japan, Boukhors expressed disbelief over the airport’s blind spots.

“I was very surprised some CCTV were not operational, not working. That’s what they told me around airport and in front of Grab and without CCTV not working. And for such a big airport, I was very surprised,” Boukhors said, adding that the pick-up area had “zero cameras.”
Mendoza noted that the airport’s CCTV system is five years old and the New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC) has started taking over some of the equipment as part of the transition to privatization.

With the anticipated influx of passengers on All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days, panel chair Sen. Raffy Tulfo issued a 48-hour ultimatum to the MIAA and NNIC to submit a comprehensive status report and ensure all cameras are functioning.
Tulfo said his public service program recovered Boukhors’ three stolen watches.
With a tipster’s help, Tulfo said authorities tracked down the suspect, identified as Raymond Sarmiento, who reportedly sold the P18-million timepieces in Baclaran for P120,000.

articles.title: Hegseth to ASEAN: Deliver peace through strength
articles.summary: United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke before his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Cebu City yesterday, where he reaffirmed the Trump administration’s…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gestures during a joint press conference with Philippines' Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro after their meeting at Camp Aguinaldo in Manila on March 28, 2025.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke before his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Cebu City yesterday, where he reaffirmed the Trump administration’s vision for a prosperous and stable Pacific “based on strength, built not on wishful thinking but on the backs of strong, self-reliant nations.”

“The approach we’re taking we describe as strong, quiet and clear. Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics and to let our actions speak for themselves, but are clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners,” Hegseth said at opening of the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers Meeting and 13th ADMM Plus.

“That is by definition peace through strength and we’re ready and willing to work with all of you where you are based on your own circumstances and your own priorities and shared mutual interests thereafter,” he said.

Hegseth noted that while the US and ASEAN member-states are “not going to agree on everything, nor do we need to,” speaking as one on fundamentals “is enough to support practical cooperation where our shared interests are overlapping and are clear, and that’s the type of cooperation the Department of War will continue to pursue with our ASEAN partners.”

He stressed that strengthening maritime domain awareness, improving interoperability and advancing cooperation among US and ASEAN navies are not symbolic things, but “are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do.”
“Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict,” he said.

“The United States is a proud Pacific nation, and alongside our ASEAN partners, we are resolved to deliver peace through strength. Peace, prosperity and sovereignty for all member-nations based on mutual respect and strength,” he maintained.

In his remarks, Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. said ASEAN values the United States’ “sustained engagement” with the region’s defense establishments, pointing out that “a robust US presence is necessary for peace and stability in Southeast Asia and in the broader Indo-Pacific region.”
He said the Philippines’ hosting of the ASEAN gathering coincided with the 80th anniversary of the establishment of the Philippines’ diplomatic ties with the US.

In May, Teodoro and Hegseth met on the sidelines of the International Institute for Strategic Studies Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore to reaffirm their ironclad commitment to the US-Philippine Mutual Defense Treaty and shared determination to ensure a stable peace in the Indo-Pacific.
Meanwhile, Hegseth’s visit was denounced by militant groups, particularly the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), which called him a war criminal undeserving of special treatment in the Philippines.
Bayan secretary general Raymond Palatino said Hegseth should be tried for violating international humanitarian rules in the US war on Iran.

articles.title: Chinese ships monitored near Panatag Shoal

The PCG, said its spokesman for the West Philippine Sea Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela, monitored the presence of the Chinese vessels on Tuesday while it was assisting the BFAR in its support mission.

“PCG Commandant Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan directed the deployment of PCG surface and air assets to secure the mission, underscoring that the protection of Filipino fishermen and the delivery of government support to them at sea remain among the priorities of the Coast Guard in the West Philippine Sea,” Tarriela said without giving further details.

Some 50 Filipino fishermen around Panatag Shoal received fuel support under the Kadiwa ng Bagong Bayaning Mangingisda Program or KBBM, allowing them to stay longer in the fishing grounds, with reduced fuel costs.
The PCG said the BFAR mission was carried out successfully and with no untoward incidents.
Tarriela underscored that the support missions for the Filipino fisherfolk are aimed at promoting food security and maritime development in the West Philippine Sea.

MANILA, Philippines — A majority of Filipinos consider the United States and Japan as the Philippines’ most important partners for economic security, a recent survey conducted by Pulse Asia showed.

articles.title: Digital apps with violent history must prove safety – Angara
articles.summary: Applications with a history of being used for violence should prove their social media platforms are safe for children, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said, amid proposals to ban minors’…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Education Secretary Sonny Angara.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Applications with a history of being used for violence should prove their social media platforms are safe for children, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said, amid proposals to ban minors’ access to “high risk digital services.”

“Definitely those apps with a history of being used for violence, being used by terrorists, nihilistic, violent, extremist groups for grooming, we should reverse the burden. Instead of them placing the burden on us to prove that they’re being used for these acts, let’s place the burden on them to prove that their app is safe for the use of our kids,” Angara said.

The Senate has passed on third and final reading the proposed “Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act,” seeking to ban minors’ access to “high risk digital services” like Roblox and GoreBox, which are online platforms where youth have been groomed into committing violent acts.
Angara said he is in favor of measures regulating internet use for minors.

“I don’t know which age, we’ll leave it to our legislators, but definitely, I think up to 15, 16, very vulnerable for them because they’re very emotional and their faculties are not fully formed. And then also, because they’re very emotional, sometimes they do something and they regret later on,” Angara said.
The bill will compel high-risk digital services to suspend, restrict, disable or remove any account owned, operated or used by anyone under 18 years old.

Not covered by the ban are electronic mail services, private messaging services, online gaming services not primarily used for social networking, educational platforms, news services and professional collaboration services.
“Because there may still be technology in educational apps and maybe communication apps,” he said.
Angara said that implementation is crucial once the proposed measure is signed into law.
“The enforcement is also something that should come into play when you pass a law because that will be partially or wholly unenforceable,” he said.

articles.title: Bernardo: Jinggoy got P573 million in kickbacks in 4 tranches
articles.summary: Former public works undersecretary and state witness Roberto Bernardo testified yesterday before the Sandiganbayan that detained Sen. Jinggoy Estrada received P573 million in kickbacks, delivered in…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Sen.Jinggoy Estrada leaves the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City after attending his scheduled arraignment on the graft case filed against him at the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City on June 2, 2026.
STAR / Miguel de Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — Former public works undersecretary and state witness Roberto Bernardo testified yesterday before the Sandiganbayan that detained Sen. Jinggoy Estrada received P573 million in kickbacks, delivered in four tranches, from infrastructure projects.
During the bail hearing of Estrada’s plunder case, Bernardo said the money was delivered from the Diamond Hotel in Manila to Estrada’s residence in San Juan.

The first delivery was in November 2024, the second in December 2024 and the third and fourth in February 2025. For the final delivery, Bernardo said he accompanied his driver in bringing 11 boxes containing P20 million to the senator’s residence.
He, however, said he has no photographs of the alleged transactions, saying he was aware that these were “illegal” and he did not need to provide documents or evidence.
Implicating a friend
During the hearing, Bernardo was asked why he did not initially name Estrada among the officials who allegedly received kickbacks in his affidavit in September 2025.
He only later accused Estrada of receiving kickbacks from infrastructure projects in November 2025 and his latest judicial affidavit on Monday.
Bernardo cited his friendship with Estrada, saying even though he already knew that the senator was a proponent of projects, he wanted to have solid evidence first before implicating a friend.
“It was difficult to implicate a friend. I couldn’t do it right away,” he said.
Bernardo pointed out that he reserved his right to execute a supplemental affidavit, if needed, due to the complex nature of the case.
Estrada personally attended the bail hearing for the first time, then asked the Sandiganbayan to allow him to return to his cell at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas.
Asked for comment on Bernardo’s testimony, Estrada said it has a lot of inconsistencies. “He implicated too many people. The testimony is full of inconsistencies.
It was clear that he never brought money to me,” said Estrada.
When asked if he considered Bernardo a friend before, the senator said he did not want to have enemies as much as possible.

articles.title: DBM: NCA utilization rate at 96.6%
articles.summary: Government agencies utilized 96.6 percent of their notices of cash allocation (NCA) as of end-September, while the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) had the largest amount of unused NCAs…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Data from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) showed that NCAs grew by 7.5 percent to nearly P4 trillion as of end-September from P3.72 trillion in the same period last year.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Government agencies utilized 96.6 percent of their notices of cash allocation (NCA) as of end-September, while the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) had the largest amount of unused NCAs at P59.19 billion.
Even with the increase, government agencies recorded a slightly lower utilization rate of 96.6 percent from 97.3 percent in the nine months in 2025.
This means that of the total releases, P3.86 trillion has been utilized and some P136.5 billion was unused as of end-September.

NCAs are disbursement orders by the DBM to government banks servicing the release of funds to agencies. State agencies are expected to use the NCAs to pay for the cash requirements of their programs and projects.
Line departments, which received the bulk of the releases, registered a utilization rate of 95.2 percent from 96.6 percent last year. They used P2.6 trillion of the P2.73 trillion released.
This leaves P130.6 billion in NCAs for the period.
By department, the DPWH had the biggest unused NCAs as of end-September.
The DPWH recorded a utilization rate of 86.7 percent from 95.6 percent last year. It used P386.07 billion of the P445.26 billion released.

The DPWH is facing stricter scrutiny over the release and use of funds after being embroiled in multibillion-peso irregularities in flood control projects, which prompted an overhaul of its leadership and budget and even procurement processes.
The Department of Education (DepEd) received the largest allocation among departments at P624.3 billion, of which P601.57 billion or 96.4 percent had been utilized.
Those that had full utilization rates include the judiciary, Commission on Audit, Commission on Elections, Office of the Ombudsman and the Commission on Human Rights.
Among agencies with lower utilization rates is the Department of Agriculture, which posted an 84.8 percent rate after using P70.11 billion of its P82.64-billion NCA allocation.

Others are the Department of Information and Communications Technology (85.1 percent rate), Civil Service Commission (81.4 percent), Office of the President (76.3 percent) and Presidential Communications Office (75.3 percent).

articles.title: PNP launches hotlines for tipsters on Bato
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police has opened five 24/7 hotlines and guaranteed confidentiality for tipsters who can provide any information on the whereabouts of wanted Sen. Ronald “Bato”…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Police display on screen the hotline numbers to receive information on Sen. Ronald dela Rosa’s whereabouts. (Inset) Senator Bato Dela Rosa.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police has opened five 24/7 hotlines and guaranteed confidentiality for tipsters who can provide any information on the whereabouts of wanted Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.

PNP spokesman Col. Allen Rae Co said the cellphone numbers are 0927-3073501, 0995-5122729, 0945-6115926, 0999-3619878 and 0960-6923025. They are operational and ready to accept calls and messages from informants who have leads on Dela Rosa.
Co added that tipsters can also use the Unified 911 hotline.
“We assure anybody who will be giving tips that their identities, numbers will be kept confidential,” Co said at a news briefing in Camp Crame.
Dela Rosa is believed to be hiding somewhere in Mindanao under the protection of a powerful armed group.

With the looming deadline for Dela Rosa to surrender, Co urged members of the senator’s family to convince him to turn himself in to the authorities, adding that they want a peaceful resolution and accord the senator dignity instead of hunting him down.
“Maybe they could talk to the senator and prevail upon him to voluntarily surrender,” Co said.
If the senator’s wife Nancy would reach out to them, Co said they would welcome the gesture.
Another person who could serve as a bridge is Dela Rosa’s son, Rock, a captain in the police force.
“It’s very hard for a son but that’s one of the avenues,” he said.
‘No political persecution’

Efforts to track down Dela Rosa do not constitute political persecution, Malacañang stressed yesterday. ?Palace press officer Claire Castro said Dela Rosa’s case started in 2017 during the term of former president Rodrigo Duterte, whose controversial drug war left more than 6,000 suspects dead based on official data.

“At that time, President Marcos Jr. was a private citizen. To claim that it is a political persecution is a bit far-fetched,” Castro told Bombo Radyo yesterday. ?Castro cited Republic Act 9851 or the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide and Other Crimes Against Humanity to justify the operations against Dela Rosa, who was chief of the PNP when Duterte launched the drug war.

Under the law, authorities may surrender or extradite suspected or accused persons in the Philippines to an appropriate international court, if any, or to another state pursuant to the applicable extradition laws and treaties.
“We did not violate any law,” Castro said.

“If this issue did not happen way, way back, the government would not surrender anyone. It just happened that there is an issue and let us not forget that there are alleged victims of EJK (extrajudicial killings) who also need justice,” she added.

Castro responded to critics who argued that no local institution has issued an arrest warrant against Dela Rosa and that surrendering the senator to the ICC is tantamount to turning over a Filipino citizen to foreigners.
She argued that the ICC is a court, not a foreign state, and that the Philippines was a member of the ICC when the case started.

“Let us not just focus on Sen. Bato and other co-perpetrators. Let us also remember as Filipinos that there are Filipinos who are crying and who have ill feelings because they feel that they have not receive enough and real justice,” Castro added.
The government has offered a P50-million bounty for the capture of the senator and has given him until tomorrow to surrender. – Alexis Romero

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy irked by US-Russia-China summit
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has voiced his concerns about a probable meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia next month. Plus, a localized truce appeared to be holding in the town of Oleshky.

image.caption: Zelenskyy is concerned that Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin could divide up global spheres of influence between themImage: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that a planned meeting between Russia, China and the United States next month could present the three participants with an opportunity to redraw global spheres of influence.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," he said in comments to journalists on Wednesday, referring to the 1945 Yalta Conference in Crimea , where Allied powers redrew the world map in the wake of the Second World War.
Putin raised idea of three-way summit with Trump: What to know

The Kremlin has previously indicated that preparations were underway for a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US and Chinese counterparts, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit next month.
The Wall Street Journal first broke the news about the three-way summit earlier this month and said that Trump had not agreed to attend the summit at the time.
But the Journal said Trump was open to the proposal — that had been raised by Putin — since he wanted to bring an end to the war in Ukraine.

"What China, Russia and the United States might discuss has not yet been clearly defined," Zelenskyy said, adding that "Russia wants this meeting more than anyone," warning against handing Moscow "another major diplomatic advantage."
For years now, Russia has been seeking a new agreement with Washington on European security architecture, and in particular an end to what Putin considers NATO's aggressive expansion towards Russia.
Putin has falsely repeatedly said Ukraine war was an act of self-defense
Putin continues to cast the ongoing invasion of Ukraine as a response to such a NATO threat – a position widely rejected in Kyiv and the rest of Europe.
Zelenskyy's warning came ahead of planned talks between Ukrainian, Russian and US envoys in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) next month.
No specific date has been set for the Abu Dhabi meeting, but Kyiv is keen for it to take place before the potential Russia-China-US summit.
Before that, it was also confirmed on Wednesday that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will travel to the United States for a meeting with G20 counterparts in Atlanta on October 30-31.

blocks.caption: Zelenskyy's comments were released as he traveled to the Netherlands for talks with Dutch Prime Minister Rob JettenImage: Remko de Waal/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Zelenskyy in Netherlands
Zelenskyy's remarks were released as he traveled to the Netherlands for meetings with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Dutch King Willem-Alexander in The Hague.
The Dutch government said on Wednesday it would provide Ukraine with €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) in non-military support over the next ⁠years.
Zelenskyy also held a phone call with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to thank him for an ​extra £10 ⁠billion ($13.29 billion/€11.94 billion) of support announced earlier ⁠on ​Wednesday.
"A truly ​strong very timely step coming right Russia needs to and ​feel that Ukraine will not be left ​alone to deal with the problems ⁠Russia ​is so ​eager to escalate," he wrote on social media.
But Ukraine's greatest assets in its defense against Russian aggression remain US Patriot air defense missiles, and Zelenskyy urged Washington to increase supplies.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been receiving 12 missiles a month this year but is being targeted with "150 ballistic missiles a month."
Oleshky truce holding for now, Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile on the battlefield, officials said a six-day ceasefire in a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine held for its first day and night.

The localized truce in the devastated town of Oleshky began on Tuesday and is due to last until Sunday, enabling a planned humanitarian operation to provide around 2,000 remaining residents with urgently needed food and medicine, and evacuate those who want to leave.
"We are grateful that they are organizing this possibility to evacuate people," said President Zelenskyy.
The plight of Oleshky in Ukraine's southern Kherson region caught the attention of US first lady Melania Trump, who the White House said helped broker the humanitarian mission.
If the ceasefire holds, it will be the first time in more than four-and-a-half years of fighting that both sides have observed a significant truce, with previous attempts quickly unraveling.
"This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," said Ukraine's negotiator, Davyd ‌Arakhamia, on Tuesday, adding every step brings peace closer.
Oleshky ceasefire comes into effect in Ukraine war
Drone attacks in Kharkiv, Belgorod — and off Bulgaria
Elsewhere, however, the war raged on with five people, including a four-year-old child, injured in a Russian drone strike on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight.

In Moscow, the Russian Defense Ministry said air defenses had downed 531 Ukrainian drones on Tuesday night and into Wednesday morning, but local authorities in the Belgorod border region said one person was killed in a drone attack.
And in Sofia, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said three maritime drones struck a container ship in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria.

The crew evacuated the vessel and there were no immediate reports of casualties, according to Bulgarian state news agency BTA, but the incident took place as defense ministers from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were meeting in Sofia for trilateral talks focused on Black Sea security.

"We follow with concern the intense attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea ​and call on the sides to act with common sense, in line with the principle of navigational safety in open seas," said Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Guler.
"The necessary warnings are constantly being conveyed to both sides to keep commercial navigational out of the conflict zone and ​immediately halt attacks on civilian vessels."
A series of drone attacks have occurred this month off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria. Russia has not taken responsibility, but suspicion has increasingly fallen on Moscow.
"The logic points in that direction," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told parliament earlier this month. "The problem is that we cannot prove it."

articles.title: In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely
articles.summary:
A movement that began in outrage has delivered remarkable election upset, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes next

•

blocks.text: In April of last year, dozens of students set off from Serbia, intent on making it to Strasbourg, France on bicycles. The aim of the arduous, 13-day transcontinental journey was simple: to make their voices heard in Europe and beyond.

In their home city of Novi Sad, students had been holding near-daily protests after a deadly roof collapse at the city’s main railway station. As their push for accountability and justice spread across the country, it was met with baton-wielding police, teargas and a political class that branded these young people as traitors.

Their trek to Strasbourg was aimed at casting a spotlight on the deepening erosion of democratic values in their home country. “Serbia needs Europe’s support,” the students explained in an open letter to the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as they arrived in Strasbourg and met with MEPs and officials. “We are not riding toward Europe to flee Serbia. We are riding to bring it back.”

On Sunday, their movement made headlines across the world as the students were catapulted from the streets of Serbia into the halls of power. In a ballot that saw the highest turnout since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992, over 50% of voters backed the students to oust the increasingly authoritarian leader, Aleksandar Vučić, and end his party’s 14 years in power.
It was, as a Guardian editorial noted, “one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history”.

The students’ extraordinary feat came as Europe has been rocked by weeks of protests. From Porto to Paris and Madrid to Milan, analysts have pointed to the common thread that weaves through the diverse protests: a view that the social contract has broken down, leaving younger generations bracing for a future in which they will be worse off than their parents.

The election result in Serbia lays bare the power of these protests to reshape politics, postdoctoral researcher Aleksandar Matković noted this week. Could it be, as WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange once told an interviewer in Belgrade, that Serbia is “a country where the future happens first”?

Matković drew on his involvement inside the student movement to offer a singular window into all that had gone into their win, citing discussions that had stretched as long as six hours as the students laid the groundwork for their entry into politics. “The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics,” he wrote.

Their win sparked joy across Serbia, sending tens of thousands of jubilant revelers on to streets across the country. “It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” Sara, 24, told the Guardian.
Hours later supporters of the movement appeared again, this time to clean up after a night of raucous celebrations.
What happens now?

blocks.caption: When the celebrations are over, the question of government begins. Photograph: Aleksandar Jovicic/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The movement now faces a tremendous task – particularly given that it has no hierarchy or leader. For more than a decade, Vučić’s party had transformed the state, tightening its grip on media, stuffing institutions with loyalists to the party and wielding ministries and Serbian institutions as political tools.
after newsletter promotion

The movement won 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, giving a comfortable majority to a slate of candidates who range from academics to athletes, and who were chosen via student assemblies in the lead-up to the election. As one candidate told my colleagues on Monday, the top priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.

Underpinning the movement is an 11-point plan, which includes ridding the country of corruption, reforming the judiciary and media and improving access to healthcare. “We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory,” one member of the movement wrote in the Guardian this week. “Rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.”

And while their plans for power take shape, the impact of their bold experiment will certainly be felt far beyond Serbia. The country applied to join the European Union in 2009, but the process has largely stalled in recent years. Now, much like in neighbouring Hungary, the elections have ushered in the possibility of a fresh start along with hope of a democratic resurgence in central Europe.

As EU officials sent their congratulations this week to the students, whose policy platform promises to put the question of future EU membership to a referendum, a note of optimism laced their messages. “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, said on social media.
Marta Kos, the EU’s enlargement commissioner, was more direct. “A new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together,” she wrote on social media.

It was a stunning reversal of fortunes for the students who last year felt they had to cycle more than 1,300km (780 miles) to make their voices heard. Now – after nearly two years of protests that were met with detentions on trumped-up evidence, illegal surveillance, threats and job losses – it seems they might have a chance to fulfil their wish of bringing Europe to Serbia.

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after fleeing Brazil for US
articles.summary: Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Florida early on Wednesday. Facing money laundering allegations, he fled just days after refusing to concede defeat…

image.caption: News of Bolsonaro departing Brazil broke on Tuesday, just two days after Brazil's presidential electionsImage: Marta Lavandier/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazilian right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami, Florida in the US on Wednesday morning.
His plan to leave Brazil became public knowledge late on Tuesday, soon after he had refused to concede defeat in Sunday's presidential elections and pledged to challenge the results.

Bolsonaro refused to comply with a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, tied to a money-laundering investigation in which he denies wrongdoing, and the US State Department later said it would grant him and his family visas.

blocks.caption: The Bolsonaro's were escorted to a vehicle under cover of umbrellas Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/REUTERS

blocks.text: When did Bolsonaro arrive, how did he reach Miami?
Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters were seen disembarking a Gulfstream G400 plane and heading into the Miami-Opa Locka airport on Wednesday morning.
Their journey across the Americas had captured regional attention.
The quartet first flew into Argentina late on Tuesday, then took a private jet to the Ecuadorean city of Guayaquil. From there, they continued to Miami in Florida.

blocks.caption: As a sitting senator Bolsonaro had immunity from prosecution but he had announced plans to give up that role to challenge Lula for the presidencyImage: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP

blocks.text: Bolsonaro would lose his immunity from prosecution in February when his term in the Senate ends. On Monday, he had said in an Instagram post that he had no intention of leaving the country and that he would "hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
According to the AFP news agency, Bolsonaro also holds Italian citizenship and so was able to travel despite his Brazilian and diplomatic passports being canceled.

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro's flights out of Brazil and towards Miami had been tracked overnightImage: Eva Marie Uzcategui/REUTERS

blocks.text: Potential source of strain between Trump's US and Lula's Brazil

Bolsonaro's departure and his arrival in Florida — like his father Jair Bolsonaro before him after Brazil's previous presidential elections — could deepen a rift between the two most populous countries in the Americas.
During the election campaign, incumbent Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva had accused the Donald Trump administration of colluding with the Bolsonaro family in a bid to help them return to power.

After the election results, Trump appeared to question the integrity of the vote, saying he thought the extension to voting times was a "very bad look." He had also alleged in the past that Jair Bolsonaro was the victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.
Bolsonaro senior is now in jail in Brazil on charges of leading a conspiracy designed to keep him in power despite defeat in 2022's presidential election.

articles.title: Israel election: what we know so far
articles.summary: With nearly all votes counted, Netanyahu’s coalition government has lost its majority, but main opponents also fail to gain outright majority; marked gains by Palestinian parties

items: With almost all votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government has lost its majority, but his main opponents, an alliance of Jewish Israeli parties unofficially led by Gadi Eisenkot, have also failed to gain an outright majority.

Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 53 seats under the current vote share, but this could change further. The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 48 seats and the Palestinian parties on 19 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset.
The remainder of votes to be counted come from absentee ballots, according to Israeli media. We can expect absentee ballots to be counted on Wednesday night, with final results by Thursday.

The Palestinian Israeli parties have received a historically strong vote. The Joint List, a new ticket of several Arab-majority parties, triumphed with at least 12 seats, while Ra’am, the other Islamic party, won seven.

The key question is whether the Eisenkot-led “Change” bloc (consisting of the rightwinger Naftali Bennett’s Together party, the centre-left Yair Golan’s Democrats and the rightwing Yisrael Beiteinu party) will partner with Palestinian Israeli parties or if they will resort to a new election, or even working with Netanyahu.

Netanyahu took the stage at a post-election rally in Jerusalem just after 3am, telling his supporters that official results will show that “Likud is the largest party in Israel”. He told his supporters that the country must “establish a strong, rightwing national government” – adding that a government that relied on the support of Palestinian parties must not be formed.

Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv that the “Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister … a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics”. In his speech, he also warned Netanyahu not to “use Israel’s security” for political ends, playing on fears that the prime minister could use this period of uncertainty to launch a new attack on Iran.

The Palestinian Israeli vote, which represents about 20% of the population, had long been seen as a decisive factor for who will be able to form government, and the high turnout of this election was driven by the community experiencing increased racism and discrimination under Netanyahu’s government.
This is the most voted-for election in Israel’s political history, with many Israelis flying back into the country to cast their vote, and nearly 80% of IDF soldiers voting.
Donald Trump said his endorsement had helped Netanyahu perform better than polling estimates.

articles.title: How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios
articles.summary: With 85% of votes counted, all signs point to an impasse. The most likely outcome may be new elections.

blocks.text: Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?
Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.

Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".
But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.

Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government"- remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.

One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.
This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.
This would be a seismic shift for Israeli politics. Only one independent Arab party has ever formally been part of a coalition, in 2021, and it didn't last long.
Eisenkot and every other Jewish party in his bloc bar one have already ruled out entering government with them. But right now, it's the opposition's only path to a majority.

The Arab parties were the story of election night. They look to have defied expectations and could gain a record 19 seats - helped by an unprecedented turnout from Israel's Arab population, who account for about one-fifth of the country and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout last night, inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, has shaken things up.

The United Arab list, who are currently projected to win around 7 seats, have said they'd join an opposition government, while The Joint List, who are projected to win 12 seats, have said they'd support one from outside.

However, the only Jewish leader advocating this scenario right now is The Democrats' Yair Golan. And a coalition like this would be very fragile, especially on issues like Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The fact there is such a unified front from the Jewish parties against Arab participation points to Israel's deep divisions.

articles.title: SAFE Kids vs. SMART Kids: Is the Philippines ready?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – I attended “SAFE Kids, SMART Policies: A Dialogue on Children’s Online Safety and Digital Rights,” organized by Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra at The Manila House on…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – I attended “SAFE Kids, SMART Policies: A Dialogue on Children’s Online Safety and Digital Rights,” organized by Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra at The Manila House on Thursday, October 22, to help get the discussion going and give the media, industry leaders, and fellow parents a better understanding of the two bills: the SAFE Kids Act and the SMART Kids Act.
The discussion raised an important question for me: beyond deciding which bill offers better protection for children, are we building a comprehensive system that can actually keep them safe online?

The conversation around children’s online safety often comes down to a comparison between restrictions and digital freedom. Which policy offers better protection? Which approach gives children more room to explore the internet while keeping them safe from its dangers?

But after considering the discussion surrounding the SAFE Kids Act and the SMART Kids Act, I find myself asking a bigger question: Are we building a comprehensive system to protect Filipino children, or are we once again trying to solve a complex problem with a partial solution?
It is easy to compare two bills and determine which one appears better on paper. It is much harder to ask whether the country is prepared to implement either of them effectively.
Beyond restrictions: Where do parents fit into the equation?

One of the most important aspects of children’s online safety is the role of parents. Yet, when we discuss legislation, the conversation often revolves around restrictions, penalties, platform accountability, and the responsibility of technology companies.
These are all important considerations. However, where in the legislation do we address the need to educate parents themselves?

Will digital parenting become part of the seminars that couples attend as they prepare for parenthood? Will it be incorporated into existing parenting programs under local government units or relevant government agencies? Will parents receive practical guidance on recognizing online exploitation, discussing sensitive digital experiences with their children, identifying misinformation, and setting healthy boundaries around technology?
And if these programs already exist, how accessible are they, and how effective have they been?

We cannot assume that every parent understands the digital environment their children are navigating. Some grew up alongside technology, while others are still learning how social media, online gaming, artificial intelligence, and digital communities work. Telling parents to protect their children without equipping them with the knowledge to do so risks making parental responsibility another obligation without adequate support.

At the end of the day, it is not just about the technology a child uses or the environment they grow up in. It is also about how informed and equipped their parents are to help them process the information they encounter.

A parent can be present, absent, supportive, neglectful, informed, or uninformed. These differences can shape how children understand and respond to the world around them. This is not about placing the entire burden of online safety on children or their parents. Rather, it is about recognizing that legislation alone cannot replace the guidance children need at home.

We also have to ask ourselves: What values are we demonstrating to our children? How do we teach accountability, critical thinking, empathy, and responsible technology use when we are still learning how to practice these things ourselves?
Protecting children must also mean educating the adults responsible for protecting them.
Digital rights must account for economic realities
Another concern is whether digital restrictions consider the realities of Filipino families.
When looking at other countries’ policies, we should consider not only online safety and education but also working-age laws, economic conditions, and the support available to families.
For some minors, the internet is more than entertainment. It can be a way to earn money, develop skills, create content, and support their families.

Consider the SMART Kids Act’s proposed blanket ban on social media access for those under 18. While protecting children from exploitation is important, treating all minors the same overlooks their different ages and circumstances.

A 16- or 17-year-old earning through legitimate content creation or creative work has different needs from a much younger child who may be more vulnerable to exploitation. If we take away these opportunities without providing alternatives, could some young people turn to less regulated or more dangerous ways to earn money?

The SAFE Kids Act’s tiered approach considers different factors, offering a way to balance children’s safety with their varying needs and circumstances. With proper safeguards, it could help distinguish harmful online activities from legitimate, age-appropriate opportunities.

Ultimately, protecting children should not mean ignoring the economic realities they face. If our goal is to prevent exploitation, we must do more than restrict access. We must also address the circumstances that make children vulnerable in the first place.
Accountability should not stop with platforms and parents

Discussions about children’s online safety understandably emphasize technology companies’ accountability. Platforms must be expected to implement appropriate safeguards, protect users’ information, respond to abuse, and take meaningful steps to prevent foreseeable harm.
Parents must also be supported in fulfilling their responsibilities. But what about the children themselves?

Accountability is an important part of growing up. Children need to understand that their actions online have consequences, whether they involve cyberbullying, harassment, spreading harmful content, violating another person’s privacy, or participating in other forms of online misconduct.

Of course, accountability must match a child’s age, maturity, circumstances, and capacity to understand the consequences of their actions. It should not mean treating children like adults or imposing punitive measures without considering their development.
Instead, the goal should be to help children understand responsibility, repair harm where possible, and learn from their mistakes.
This raises another question: If we are strengthening the rules that govern children’s digital behavior, are we also prepared to strengthen the systems that teach and enforce accountability?

The Philippines already has a juvenile justice framework under Republic Act No. 9344, as amended by Republic Act No. 10630. However, the existence of a law does not automatically mean that its implementation is adequate, accessible, or consistently effective.

Before adding another layer of restrictions, we should examine whether existing juvenile justice, intervention, rehabilitation, and educational systems are sufficiently equipped to address the realities of digital misconduct.

How do we ensure that a child who causes harm online receives appropriate consequences while also having an opportunity to learn and rehabilitate? How do we protect victims without overlooking the developmental needs of children who commit offenses?

These questions deserve attention alongside the discussion of digital restrictions. Otherwise, we risk creating rules without adequately preparing the institutions responsible for putting them into practice.
Why are we moving forward when the broader legal framework still has gaps?
We must also look beyond legislation specifically designed for children and acknowledge the gaps in our existing online safety laws.

Filipinos continue to face online scams, identity theft, harassment, fraud, and privacy violations. While the Philippines has laws covering cybercrime, data privacy, and online transactions, having these laws in place does not automatically mean that victims are adequately protected.

Challenges remain in public awareness, reporting mechanisms, law enforcement, and the investigation of increasingly complex online offenses. Many Filipinos may not know where to report incidents or what steps to take when they become victims. Meanwhile, technology continues to evolve, creating new risks that existing laws and enforcement systems may struggle to address.

These gaps raise a bigger concern: are we doing enough to strengthen our existing legal framework and the institutions responsible for enforcing it? Passing legislation is only the first step. Effective implementation requires funding, coordination among government agencies, public education, and consistent enforcement.

If we want to make the digital world safer for children, we must also address the weaknesses in the systems meant to protect everyone online. Child protection cannot exist in isolation from the country’s broader cybersecurity and online safety efforts.
The bigger question: Are we building a system or applying a band-aid?
Comparing the SAFE Kids Act and the SMART Kids Act is only the beginning. The bigger question is whether our country is ready to implement these policies effectively.

Passing a law is one thing. Educating parents, involving schools and local governments, funding enforcement, and ensuring that children’s digital rights are protected are different challenges altogether.

We also need to consider whether our existing cybersecurity and online safety systems are equipped to support these new policies. If gaps in enforcement, public awareness, and existing laws remain unresolved, introducing another law may not be enough.

Protecting children requires more than restrictions. It requires digital literacy, educated parents, accountable platforms, accessible reporting systems, and support for families. We must also ensure that children understand their responsibilities online and that policies do not unintentionally harm those who rely on legitimate digital opportunities.

Yes, the point is to make our kids safer. But are we prepared to make these policies work, or are we simply applying another band-aid solution to the country’s existing online safety and cybersecurity problems?

Comparing the two bills is one thing. Building a system that can effectively protect Filipino children is another. Our responsibility does not end with passing a law. It begins with making sure that the law actually works.
As a future parent, I cannot rely on legislation alone
Perhaps the most personal part of this conversation is realizing that, as a future parent, I will still have to prepare my child for an imperfect digital world.
I will have to teach them how to recognize harmful information, question what they see online, protect their privacy, respect other people, and ask for help when something does not feel right.
I will have to explain that not everything they encounter online is true, that not everyone they meet has good intentions, and that technology can be useful without always being safe.

I will also have to make sure they understand that restrictions are not substitutes for judgment. Eventually, children grow older, gain independence, and make decisions without their parents watching over them. The goal cannot simply be to keep them away from every possible danger. It must also be to prepare them to recognize and respond to danger when it appears.
And I know that the responsibility will not fall on me alone. Schools, communities, technology companies, and the government all have a role to play.

But the reality is that these institutions will have limitations. Laws may have loopholes. Platforms may fail to detect harmful content. Reporting systems may not always work as expected. Technology will continue to evolve faster than regulations can reasonably keep up.
As a parent, I cannot assume that every gap will be addressed before my child encounters it.

That is why parental education, digital literacy, and a culture of accountability matter just as much as the restrictions themselves. We need to raise children who can navigate the digital world, not simply children who have been temporarily shielded from it.

articles.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
articles.summary: Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40%

blocks.text: Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long ranked as a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety.
Officials said at least 64 people were killed on Wednesday morning after two trains collided, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were carrying 544 passengers.

While the cause of the accident has yet to be confirmed, a source told Reuters that a train operated by the private company Iryo had come to a halt near the city of Toledo because of a signalling fault and on orders from infrastructure manager Adif. Soon after, a second train, operated by state-owned Renfe struck the stationary train. It had been travelling on the same line at a high speed.
Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”.
The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

blocks.caption: A Guardia Civil officer collects evidence at the site of January’s fatal rail crash near Adamuz in Andalucía. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP

blocks.text: Media on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network.
The first crash sparked a wider conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued.

Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” the union said earlier this month.

Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.”
It has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo.

The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country where travel by train accounts for about 57% of all transport.

Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain.
The government says it has increased spending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of the 2013 crash near Santiago de Compostela that claimed 80 lives. It remains Spain’s worst rail disaster.  Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Spain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU.
Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.

Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials.

Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU.
Spain’s worst rail accident took place in 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

articles.title: Philip Lustre seeks transfer of cyber libel case from Davao City
articles.summary: The camp of veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., on Wednesday said they will ask that the cyber libel case against him be transferred from Davao City.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 10:23pm
The camp of veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., on Wednesday said they will ask that the cyber libel case against him be transferred from Davao City.

“For the court, we are in the course of filing the necessary pre-arraignment remedies including a motion for reinvestigation, motion to quash, and to of course transfer the venue because we do not feel safe in Davao City,” Lustre's lawyer Dino De Leon said in a press briefing.
He added that this is “considering the known proclivity of the Duterte family for violence.”
Police officers arrested Lustre in Quezon City on Saturday on the strength of a cyber libel arrest warrant issued by a court in Davao City.
De Leon later said that the complainant is lawyer Manases Carpio, the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Lustre has been temporarily released after posting bail.
De Leon said he has also asked Davao City Prosecutor Jhopee Avanceña to confirm her ties to Honeylet Avanceña, the partner of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag earlier said that Jhopee Avanceña and Honeylet Avanceña are cousins.

“Kami talaga ay nagugulat na pinirmahan niya ito kung related talaga siya kay Honeylet na kinakasama, longtime partner, in fact the de facto first lady nung mga panahon ni Rodrigo Duterte,” De Leon said.
(We are really surprised that he signed this, if he is indeed related to Honeylet, his live-in partner, longtime partner, and in fact, the de facto first lady during Rodrigo Duterte’s time.)
“We are asking for the record and, formally, we already wrote to the city prosecutor to confirm his relationship with Honeylet Avanceña,” he added.
He said they are also asking the prosecutor’s office for proof of service that subpoenas and summons were sent to Lustre.
De Leon said they are also asking the prosecutor’s office to show the efforts made to determine Lustre’s correct address.

Lustre’s camp previously said it was looking into what appeared to be a violation of his right to due process during the preliminary investigation, as he had neither been served nor received a subpoena or notice.

Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon also said that Lustre was denied due process because he was not given the opportunity to respond to the complaint before an arrest warrant was issued against him. — BM, GMA News
