articles.title: [Mind the Gap] In chaotic US midterm polls, Filams are running
articles.summary: Filipinos running across statewide and local races find themselves navigating an American political system increasingly resembling tactics they thought they had left behind

blocks.text: It’s hard not to feel that this November 2026 US midterm elections is a déjà vu of cheating in Philippine elections.

“Dinaya!” is usually the first word a losing candidate shouts in the Philippines: “I got cheated!” President Donald Trump seems to have taken this script to heart, casting a shadow over the forecasted “Blue Wave” that could flip Congress to Democratic control even before the first ballot is counted.

Even if Trump’s unfounded claims of voter fraud are overwhelmed by a huge Democratic turnout, many fear that Republicans in Congress, out of loyalty to Trump, may try to block Democrats from assuming the majority.

Echoing the “doomsday scenario” espoused by US Attorney General Todd Blanche — delaying the count or refusing to certify results if they favor Democrats — Trump has directed the Justice Department to block certification of the coming Senate election in Alaska if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses by a narrow margin. The New York Times reported that the justice department cited flimsy concerns about confusion with another candidate whose name is similar to Sullivan’s.

Their efforts to project a narrative of widespread noncitizen voting is also relentless, even using as bogeymen the 11 individuals the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) who were arrested in California on October 16 for allegedly illegally registering to vote. Election experts have raised questions as to whether the charges could be trusted to be accurate, citing similar accusations being disproved elsewhere in the country.

Remember when Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo called “Hello, Garci!” to pad her votes during the 2004 presidential election against the late Fernando Poe Jr.? Trump seems to have taken a page from that “Dagdag-Bawas” playbook by questioning voter registrations, challenging mail-in ballots and raising the possibility of hacking voting machines.

“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any election results they don’t like,” a former Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) official told ProPublica, which reported that DHS has asked CISA to “secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.”

With early voting underway, shaving off Democrat votes is in play, with software glitches delaying nearly 600,000 voter registrations in Texas. In Nashville, Tennessee, Dolly Parton’s sister, singer Stella Parton, claimed she had to correct her ballot multiple times, saying a voting machine repeatedly selected Republican gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn when she tried to vote for Democrat Jerri Green.

While a seasoned “trapo” in the Philippines rolls a ₱1,000 note in a folded T-shirt to buy votes, Trump is dangling $5,000 to voters and billions in federal aid to farmers affected by tariffs if Republicans keep control of Congress.

While hired armed goons in the Philippines steal ballot boxes, Trump has threatened to send heavily-armed ICE agents and National Guard troops to polling places, raising fears of intimidation among immigrant and minority voters. Though we are hopefully far from the impunity of an “Ampatuan massacre,” the shocking, pre-dawn DHS raid on Representative Ilhan Omar’s home three weeks before election day smacks of the same tactic in eliminating his political enemies.

Amid this chaos, Filipino candidates running across statewide and local races find themselves navigating an American political system increasingly resembling tactics they thought they had left behind.

This year’s crop includes California Attorney General Rob Bonta, seeking reelection; Assemblymember Jessica Caloza, fighting to retain her 52nd District seat; and Cerritos City Councilmember Mark Pulido, campaigning for the 67th Assembly District in the California state legislature.

In Daly City, Councilmember Rod Daus-Magbual is running for reelection, joined by Tony Bayudan in what is often celebrated as the “Pinoy Capital” of the United States, where Filipinos make up a full third of the population. In Southern California, Artesia Councilmember Melissa Ramoso is defending her seat while Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia seeks a second term.
The Filipino political footprint extends beyond California.

In Nevada, Assemblymember Erica Mosca is seeking reelection. In New York, Assemblymember Steven Raga is running for State Senate in Queens, while Georgia State Representative Marvin Lim is running unopposed.

Across the Pacific, Hawaii — the first state to elect a Filipino governor in US history with the landmark 1994 election of Benjamin Cayetano — has its own growing crop of FilAm candidates. State Senator Joy A. San Buenaventura is seeking reelection in Puna, joined by State House candidates including Tess Abalos, Travis Bumanglag, Danny Degracia, Diamond Garcia, Greggor Ilagan, Darius K. Kila, Rose Martinez and Julie Reyes Oda.

blocks.caption: 4 ways US foreign policy could change if Democrats win in November

blocks.text: At the county level, Tyler Dos Santos-Tam is seeking another term on the Honolulu City Council, while Kauanoe Batangan and Addison Bulosan are running for county council seats on Maui and Kauai.
It’s time for us to walk precincts, man phone banks and donate to our kababayan running for office.

We immigrated to the United States to escape the feudal dynasties, vote-buying and the “Guns, Goons and Gold” of traditional Philippine politics. Now it’s time to push back and make sure those tactics don’t follow us here.
So, don’t forget to vote. If voting in person, carefully review your selections before submitting your ballot to make sure the machine properly records your choice.
If voting by mail, don’t wait until November 3 to mail your ballots to prevent the understaffed US Postal Service from throwing them away if they don’t get picked up on Election Day.

In one of the most consequential elections in modern history, our mission this November is not only in supporting our kababayan to win — it is a front-line battle to make sure our votes are counted, and defend them if need be. – Rappler.com
Oscar Quiambao is a former reporter for The Philippine Daily Inquirer who now lives in San Francisco.

articles.title: Safe but excluded: Bureaucratic hurdles keep refugee kids from Gaza out of Alberta schools
articles.summary: Community advocates say they’ve seen families wait anywhere from 40 days to seven months to get their work permits, which Alberta requires before kids can be enrolled in school as local residents.

image.caption: Palestinian refugee Yousef Ziad, 8, arrived in Calgary three weeks ago. He’s excited for snow, but discouraged at the uncertain wait he faces before he can enrol in school. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

blocks.text: Refugees from Gaza are facing a months-long wait for a work permit when they arrive in Canada, which in Alberta means their children are not eligible for free enrolment in public school.
Advocates say it’s different from the process experienced by other waves of refugees — Ukrainians, Afghans and Syrians.
“I know how the system works because we have been seeing different groups of refugees come in,” said Saima Jamal, co-founder of the Calgary Immigrant Support Society.

“With the Ukrainians, right on arrival in the airport, they were given the three-year visitors’ visa and their work permit was there ... everything was all sealed and delivered to them right on arrival in the airport."
But Jamal said with “the families that started arriving from Gaza, it was a much darker scenario.”

“The wait times for a simple work permit, it’s taking like three times longer than it used to and it affects these kids so badly because they're just sitting there,” she said. “These kids are sitting at home, not being able to do anything. And the parents can't work.”

items: Hundreds of undocumented Alberta students at risk of losing free access to school

blocks.text: In Calgary, Jamal and members of the local Palestinian Community Association say they’ve seen families wait anywhere from 40 days to seven months to get their work permits. They said five months is common.
'Each crisis is different'
To understand why the experiences of the two groups differed, CBC News reached out to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. We asked for the rationale and the average wait times.
In a written statement, spokesperson Anahita Beladi said the process for the Palestinians is different because “each crisis is different.”
She declined to provide estimates for how long families wait, saying it varies with each application.
Nasser Yaghi, 11, shows the drawings he did during the months he waited at home in Calgary before he could attend school. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

The wait for work permits affects families differently across the country. Provinces such as British Columbia and Ontario allow children to attend school if their families normally reside in the province, regardless of the family’s immigration status.
Alberta requires work permit for school registration

Alberta requires a valid work or study permit for school registration, and community advocates say school boards started to enforce that rule more strictly about two years ago. Now, in addition to children not being able to register for school, they are being de-registered if their parents’ immigration permit runs out, even if the new permit is in progress.
The alternative is for the family to pay international student rates of $13,500 per child per year.

These challenges are unrelated to Alberta’s recent referendum, which could restrict access to public education further. One question asked if Alberta residents with temporary immigration status should pay a fee to access services, including education. That question passed with 52 per cent support.

Ziad Mohammed, Yasmin Talal and their two children arrived in Calgary three weeks ago. Mohammed had been a journalist in Gaza until it became too dangerous, then he opened a small pastry café. When that was destroyed in the war, the family fled to Egypt.

From left to right, Luna Zaid, Yousef Zaid and Yasmin Talal look out the window of their new Calgary apartment. They've been excited to see all the trees and wildlife, such as squirrels, in their neighbourhood. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

Talal said the conversation on the flight to Canada was all about how her eight-year-old son, Yousef Zaid, would finally get to go to school. He’s never been to school because first there was the COVID-19 pandemic, then the war, and then the family had no status in Egypt.
She had been so hopeful for Canada and was shocked to find there were still more barriers, she said through a translator.
“He needs to socialize with kids his age. He needs to be out and about. He needs to acquire the language.”
'We had no other options'
The family found a rental apartment on the far north edge of Calgary. Also using a translator, Yousef said he loves seeing the squirrels and trees, and proudly showed off his new snow boots.
For now, he’s still enrolled in the same half-day online class he was taking in Egypt, and Talal wakes him up at 6 a.m. to accommodate the time zone.
Her daughter, Luna Zaid, has completed one year of university education in engineering.

Volunteers from the local Palestinian community have suggested they check out the local library for English conversation clubs, since there is also an estimated nine-month wait for federal English lessons.
Despite the setbacks, they are happy to be in Canada, Talal said.

“We had no other options. We couldn't go back to Gaza. Everything is destroyed. Our livelihood is completely gone. In Egypt, it's not even an option to stay there because we're illegal there. So even knowing that he wouldn't be going to school right away, I would still make the decision to come here.”

Ziad Mohammed serves Arabic coffee and pastries at his new home in Calgary. He was a journalist in Gaza before that became too dangerous, then became a pastry chef and café owner. He fled with his family to Egypt after the business was destroyed in the war. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Hardest part is waiting to make friends, says 11-year-old
In Calgary’s Royal Oak neighbourhood, another family of Palestinian refugees had to wait three and a half months. But they’re glad that part of the ordeal has ended.

Nasser Yaghi, 11, said the hardest part of waiting was not having friends. He stayed at home, challenging himself to watch movies in English rather than Arabic to start training his ear. He also spent a lot of time drawing, and when he felt down, he would watch comedies with his mom.
He was finally able to join a Grade 5 class in November 2025, and now he speaks some English.
“I [felt] sad because I [didn’t] have somebody to play with, but I go to school. I am happy because I have friends. I play and I'm happy in school,” he said.

Nasser’s father, Rajab Yaghi, was an accountant who owned a tire shop in Gaza. His home, business and the four cars on site were all bombed, so the family fled to Egypt. He now has a two-year work permit and is driving for Uber.
Rajab Yaghi and his son Nasser in their apartment in northwest Calgary. Rajab owned a tire shop in Gaza before it was destroyed in the war. Now he drives for Uber. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Gaza program provides temporary haven

Jamal, with the Calgary Immigrant Support Society, is originally from Bangladesh. She came as an international student about 30 years ago and got involved with humanitarian work during the Syrian refugee crisis in 2015, when Canada welcomed 44,000 individuals in roughly one year.
She said the Syrian and later the Afghan refugees were welcomed under Canada's refugee program and given permanent residency status on arrival.

In contrast, when Canada welcomed 300,000 Ukrainians, they were offered three-year, temporary visitor visas. The Palestinian refugees are also being offered temporary visas; the federal government capped their numbers at 5,000. In both cases, they can apply for permanent residency, but there are limited spots available.
On what planet does it make sense for these refugee kids to be not going to school.Saima Jamal, Calgary Immigrant Support Society
Jamal believes politics around this particular war, as well as a shift in Canadian attitudes toward immigrants generally, is playing out in how Palestinian refugees are treated.

“There’s a culture shift now blaming everything on immigrants,” she said. “I see what’s going on in Gaza and I see the insane disparity, the double standard between how these ones are getting treated versus [the ones who came before].”

items: She fled Ukraine to safety in Alberta. Now, she’s worried about her place after the referendum

blocks.text: “On what planet does it make sense for these refugee kids to be not going to school, learning English and integrating into Canadian society?”

In July 2026, the federal government tweaked the program to allow Palestinian refugees to apply for an extension when their work permits run out. Newly arrived refugees from Gaza will also have the fees for their work or study permits waived. The program is set to expire in December 2027.

articles.title: Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?
articles.summary: Seagrass protects coasts, shelters thousands of species and stores CO2. But some 30% of this valuable ecosystem has disappeared since the late 19th century. Can we bring it back?

image.caption: Regrowing underwater seagrass meadows takes time and patienceImage: Geomar

blocks.text: Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, says she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.
How seagrass is becoming a green building material
Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.
"That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped."
Why should we care about seagrass?

Underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.
Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.
On patrol with Mallorca's 'seagrass police'
"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance."

But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.
How can seagrass be replanted on a larger scale?
Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.
"Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he said.

blocks.caption: The pressed strand of seagrass with biodegradable thread makes it easier to plant on longer stretches along the ocean floorImage: DW

blocks.text: The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.
"We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig said.
Could planting seeds be a solution?
Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing new ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.
Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.
"Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.
"The big advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

blocks.caption: Together with replanted shoots, seeds can help regrow underwater meadowsImage: DW

blocks.text: Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity."
It takes time to see results
Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.
They then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the new crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.
"We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen said. "It's looking really good."
This article is based on a Global Us video report.

articles.title: DepEd welcomes parents helping secure schools
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) on Wednesday welcomed proposals for parents to help patrol schools as authorities step up security measures following a series of school shootings in recent months.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 6:39pm

The Department of Education (DepEd) on Wednesday welcomed proposals for parents to help patrol schools as authorities step up security measures following a series of school shootings in recent months.

In a media interview, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said parental involvement in school security could also help address other concerns affecting students, including mental health and social media use.

“Welcome po sa amin yun. Dahil pinapakita yun na involved sila dito sa paaralan at pagka-nandito sila as security, magiging concerned din sila sa ibang bagay, yung mental health, yung paggamit ng social media, so wine-welcome natin yung tulong ng ating mga parents at yan talaga ang pakay ng Kaagapay program po natin,” he said.

(We welcome that because it shows that parents are involved in the school. When they participate in security efforts, they also become concerned about other matters, such as mental health and social media use. We welcome their help, as that is the purpose of our Kaagapay program.)
The Kaagapay program is a DepEd initiative aimed at encouraging greater parental involvement in their children's learning and development.

Angara made the statement after inspecting Lakan Dula High School in Tondo, Manila, as part of a school safety audit. He described the school as a model for safety, citing its security cameras, metal detectors and medical equipment.
The school also has a community drop box and a QR (quick response) code through which students and teachers can anonymously report their concerns.
The agency has since strengthened school safety and security protocols in response to the incidents of school-related violence.

In June, two students reportedly opened fire on their classmates at a high school in Tacloban, killing three people. Less than two months later, another school shooting in Zamboanga City left two students dead.
In September, a student shot two schoolmates before turning the gun on himself in South Cotabato.
The incidents shocked a country where school shootings have been extremely rare. The government has cited online groomers and nihilistic violent extremism as possible factors behind the attacks.
According to Angara, coordination with social media platform Meta was still ongoing following the incidents.
He also urged parents to take an active role in their children's lives at home.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: EU's 'Made in Europe' push unnerves global auto suppliers
articles.summary: In shielding Europe's carmakers from Chinese rivals, the EU risks hurting close partners from Turkey and Morocco to Japan and South Korea. Billions in trade and hundreds of thousands of European jobs…

image.caption: As well as supplying vehicles and parts to the EU, Turkey is making its own electric carsImage: Murat Cetinmuhurdar/Turkish Presidency/HandoutAA/picture alliance

blocks.text: It is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices. The European Union's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), proposed in March, seeks to upgrade European car factories and only subsidize vehicles produced in Europe.

Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" plan is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains.

After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?
Close to Europe, but not close enough
Other key players in the automotive sector, however, will be excluded — including Turkey, which has enjoyed seamless access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.

While the proposals still face major legislative hurdles in Brussels before becoming law, Ayhan Zeytinoglu, chairman of the Economic Development Foundation (IKV), thinks the Franco-German framework could be devastating for Turkey's auto sector.

"73% of Turkey’s total automotive exports go to the EU," Zeytinoglu told DW. "If we encounter a 'Made in Europe' barrier in the EU market, this will cause great damage to our trade with the EU and to our exports."
Excluding Turkey would also harm European automaking rather than strengthen competitiveness against China, he added.
Turkey's auto exporters association OIB calculated that the country's automotive exports to the EU totaled $30.1 billion (€26.8 billion) last year.
Protecting auto parts made in Europe
The IAA requires that 70% of the total value of a vehicle's components — excluding the battery — should be made in Europe.
However, the initial proposal only applies to battery-electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids and fuel-cell models, which last year made up just 27% of all new EU car registrations.

Tommaso Pardi, director of the international automotive research network GERPISA and a senior researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), notes that the 70% target is remarkably generous.
"If you take an average European-made electric car and take away the battery, you would find that around 83% [of parts] come from Europe," Pardi told DW.
Under the revised German-French plan, some self-charging hybrids and petrol and diesel vehicles could still be sold after 2035 and would also be affected by the "Made in Europe" rules.
These cars contain a much lower proportion of European parts. Most of Turkey's nearly 800,000 vehicle exports to the EU last year would fall under this much larger umbrella.
Europe's EV battery problem: Can it catch up with China?
China seeks a side entrance
Another key reason for excluding Turkey is that Chinese automakers are expanding their presence there, hoping to gain back-door access to the EU market, but face major roadblocks.
They include SWM Motors, whose factory in the northwestern city of Eskisehir closed within a year because the cars produced didn't meet EU safety standards.
BYD's plans to open a $1 billion plant in Manisa — a large industrial hub near the Aegean coast — have been put on hold.

Morocco, meanwhile, has received Chinese investments worth more than €10 billion ($11 billion) since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to consultancy AlixPartners, much of it in batteries and auto parts.

For France, the North African nation plays a similar role to China for Germany's auto sector — a low-cost production hub that helps French carmakers stay competitive. Budget-friendly French models would likely become more expensive if Morocco were excluded.

Japanese carmakers, which build several of their models in European factories, could also lose out. Cars imported from Japan would not qualify for EU subsidies, while models built in France, Portugal and Eastern Europe would benefit only if enough of their parts come from Europe.

South Korean automakers, meanwhile, could also be hurt. Hyundai and Kia build cars in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, but also ship models from Asia, which would not qualify. Korean battery plants in Poland and Hungary, however, would count as European.

blocks.caption: Morocco's auto plants are helping keep the costs of French car brands downImage: Renault/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Carmakers fight to keep cheap imports
Pardi notes how European car giants are actively lobbying to water down the IAA to protect their high profit margins.
"They want to limit the IAA to retain the biggest scope to still source from abroad, particularly from China," he said.
EU-based automakers warn that higher parts costs would put them at an even bigger disadvantage against Chinese rivals, while European battery supply is unlikely to meet demand anytime soon.
Ankara is also lobbying Brussels to be included in the "Made in Europe" scheme, while automakers are seeking a compromise that would allow Turkey to join at a later stage.
Pardi said this would be "only for European companies that are based there [Turkey and Morocco] ... while excluding all recent investments involving Chinese capital [in those countries]."
EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure
'Stop the bleeding' say auto parts suppliers

European auto-parts suppliers are, however, on the opposite side of the argument, calling for further strengthening of IAA. They warn that up to 650,000 auto jobs in the region could be lost by 2035 without better protection for their members.

"A lost industrial job is very hard to win back, and the damage reaches well beyond large suppliers," Benjamin Krieger, Secretary General of the European Association of Automotive Suppliers (CLEPA), told DW.
Krieger thinks the IAA helps European industry to level the playing field against unfair competition from China, adding: "We must stop the bleeding."

With broad public support for measures that ensure that EU public funding "benefits value creation in Europe," CLEPA's Krieger thinks allies like Turkey, Morocco, South Korea and Japan may not lose out if they meet the EU's criteria.

"The EU should offer access to the IAA through an opt-in mechanism with objective criteria: regulatory alignment, social and environmental standards, no market distortion, respect for the rule of law and reciprocity, backed by anti-circumvention measures. Partners that meet them are welcome," he said.
Additional reporting by Aram Ekin Duran.

articles.title: Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
articles.summary: The energy minister described it as a "major milestone" for the East African nation.

blocks.text: "The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.
Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.
In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.
Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.
Tanzania made its first natural gas discovery in 1974 on the Songo Songo Island in the south-east Lindi region, followed by a second discovery at Mnazi Bay in neighbouring region of Mtwara in 1982.

The commercialisation of these discoveries began in 2004. This propelled further gas exploration both onshore and offshore, with the largest single discovery of 2.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 2016.

articles.title: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says
articles.summary: Authorities say the attacker in Belgrade was an underage male who was being monitored by security services.

blocks.text: Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".

The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.
Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".
Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.

Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level – meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.
The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.
Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.
Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.
This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.
The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.
Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

articles.title: At least 10 dead in crash between 2 trains in central Spain, authorities say
articles.summary: A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 10 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.

image.caption: The scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday. Local authorities say at least 10 people have died, but the figure is expected to rise. (Juanma Jimenez/Europa Press/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Breaking
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 10 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region, said authorities can confirm 10 deaths, but that "that number will surely rise."
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

items: Death toll climbs to 39 in high-speed train collision in Spain

blocks.text: The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that passengers had been injured and that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.
The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, wrote on X that he is on his way to the crash site.

In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

articles.title: Vapes and cigarettes? Cop denies knowledge of Laos drug shipment try
articles.summary: The policewoman who was reportedly linked with the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of shabu from Laos to the Philippines said she had no knowledge that the shipment contained illegal drugs.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 6:11pm
The policewoman who was reportedly linked with the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of shabu from Laos to the Philippines said she had no knowledge that the shipment contained illegal drugs.

During the Senate committee on public services, Police Master Sergeant Aileen Jane Mendoza admitted that she looked for an aircraft that could be rented to transport the cargo, but she believed it only contained vapes and cigarettes.
Senator Raffy Tulfo, chairperson of the committee, asked the police officer if she knew that such shipment was illegal.
"Ang alam ko po, Mr. Chair, may kaukulang requirements po na magbabayad po kung sino ang consignee dito sa atin sa Pilipinas," said Mendoza, who attended the hearing online.
(What I know, Mr. Chair, is that there were corresponding requirements that must be paid by the consignee here in the Philippines.)

"Wala naman pong facilitation na nangyari sa ginawa ko. Ang ginawa ko po kasi, naghanap po ako ng aircraft na mare-rentahan. Regarding sa facilitation, hindi na po kasi ako ang taong in charge du'n after ko maghanap ng aircraft," she added.
(There was no facilitation in what I did. What I did was look for an aircraft to rent. After that, my job was done and I was no longer in charge of the facilitation.)
Mendoza also said she did not inform her supervisor, Police Colonel Joanna Zarcilla, regarding the chartered flight that was supposed to arrive in Manila from Laos.
Tulfo said Zarcilla should be investigated as well, while recommending her suspension pending the result of the probe.
The senator expressed belief that there may be a conspiracy among those involved in the processing of chartered flights.

"Ang pinag-uusapan natin dito ay bilyon—P3.54 billion. Hindi ako maniniwala na walang sabwatan dito hanggang sa kataas-taasan diyan kung saan mang ahensyang involved sa pag-process nitong chartered flights," Tulfo said.
(We are talking about billions here—P3.54 billion. I won't believe that there is no collusion, all the way to the very top, within the agencies involved in the processing of these chartered flights.)
"Hindi ako maniniwala na 'yung sarhento lamang ang involved. Meron pa," he added.
(I won't believe that only the sergeant is involved. There are other more.)

To recall, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla identified the Mindanao politician allegedly involved in the attempted drug smuggling as former Bangsamoro Parliament member Edriezan Hadji Nasser Rimbang.
Remulla had said Rimbang allegedly paid Mendoza for the landing rights and the private hangar where the plane was supposed to land from Laos in the last week of September.
Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Mendoza has been relieved from her post and is now under restrictive custody at the Aviation Security Group.
Rimbang, meanwhile, denied involvement in the attempted drug smuggling. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: A US woman feared dead was reported alive in Mexico. But cops now say that isn’t true
articles.summary:
Mexican police had said they found Shayna Feinman in Tijuana, raising the hopes of missing Arizonan’s family

Arizona authorities say…

blocks.text: Arizona authorities say their Mexican counterparts were resoundingly mistaken when they publicly claimed recently that they found alive a woman who was feared slain after disappearing in 2024 – a turn of events that her sister has called “turmoil” and “heartbreaking”.
The case in question centers on Shayna Feinman, who was reported missing in rural Yavapai county, Arizona, in March 2024 at age 38.

Authorities believe she was walking to an acquaintance’s home when she was last seen – but she never arrived or returned to her dog, as the Arizona news outlet KSAZ reported. An ensuing search turned up Feinman’s car abandoned near where she had been staying with her boyfriend, Cavett Richards, according to the station.
Her wallet and identification reportedly were inside the vehicle, and her cellphone was ultimately recovered on nearby land.

Although Feinman had not been found, the Yavapai county sheriff’s office subsequently charged Richards as well as a man named William DalCerro with second-degree murder, conspiracy and concealing a corpse in connection with her disappearance. But the charges were dismissed, a $20,000 reward being offered for information as authorities kept investigating the case.

blocks.caption: The person who Mexican officials thought was Shayna Feinman. Photograph: SSPCM Tijuana

blocks.text: The secretariat for security and citizen protection in the Mexican municipality of Tijuana then delivered what initially appeared to be a startling update in Feinman’s case on Saturday, saying in a statement that she had been located in the city’s Encino neighborhood the previous day.

The statement from the secretariat had a picture of the woman sitting in front of a desk atop which was a missing poster with Feinman’s information. It asserted without elaborating that investigators had confirmed Feinman’s identity, noting that her physical characteristics matched those listed in her missing person report.

The woman had been put in protective custody while Tijuana authorities arranged for her to speak with the Feinman family and US consular officials, the statement said. The agency went so far as to post a link to its Saturday statement on a social media page belonging to Feinman’s sister, Kara.
But both Kara Feinman and the Yavapai’s sheriff’s office met the Tijuana officials’ statement with evident skepticism.
Kara told KSAZ in a story published on Monday that she was waiting for the Yavapai sheriff’s office “to know for certain” that Shayna had been found.

Though she acknowledged the woman in the picture released by Tijuana officials had “similar physical attributes” to Shayna, Kara struck a cautious tone, telling KSAZ: “I can only hope and pray [for] good news – but right now, we have to be realistic.”

Meanwhile, a sheriff’s office spokesperson told KSAZ that the agency was “aware of reports indicating that Shayna Feinman may have been located in Mexico” – but “at this time, the information remains unconfirmed”.

“There is insufficient evidence to verify her identity,” Yavapai sheriff’s office spokesperson Paul Wick added to KSAZ. Wick said the sheriff’s office was “actively investigating the matter” and would provide an update as soon as one could be “confirmed and … released”.

The Yavapai sheriff’s office published that update on Tuesday, when it said in a statement: “Today, US authorities confirmed to [office] detectives, utilizing physical evidence, that the individual located is not Shayna Feinman.”

The sheriff’s office alluded to prior media reports “regarding the alleged discovery of Shayna Feinman” that “were published without official law enforcement confirmation” – before saying its “detectives continue to work diligently with [her] family during this stressful time”.
Tijuana’s security and citizen protection secretariat did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In an interview with the Guardian on Tuesday, Kara Feinman said she believed the confusion about her sister possibly being in Tijuana initially stemmed from at least one concerned citizen who became convinced that she was there and made that known on social media.

She described being guarded about that possibility, reluctantly opening her mind in light of the Tijuana secretariat’s claims – and then enduring cyberbullying online by users who harshly judged her for not reacting effusively enough to the ultimately false news that Shayna had been found alive.

As she processed the reality that the search for the truth about her sister’s disappearance continued, Kara Feinman said her hope now was for those passionate about such investigations to realize how harmful it can be “jumping to conclusions without having all of the information” and then directing harsh words at the people most affected by those cases.
“Words are stronger than people think, and kindness can go so far,” Kara Feinman said. “It’s been turmoil going through this.
“It’s heartbreaking. It’s terrible, and I don’t wish this on anybody.”

articles.title: Polls open across Manitoba for the 'wonderful opportunity' to vote in municipal elections
articles.summary: Municipal election day is underway across Manitoba. Voting locations are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.

image.caption: Manitobans will choose their next mayors, councillors and school trustees on Wednesday. (John Woods/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Municipal election day is underway across Manitoba. Voting locations are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Eligible voters can cast ballots for mayors, councillors, school trustees
Manitobans are headed to the polls in municipal elections across most of the province.

Voting locations are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. for casting ballots for mayors (or reeves, as the head of council is known in many rural municipalities), councillors and school trustees in the majority of Manitoba's 137 municipalities.

A general municipal election happens every four years and always on the third Wednesday in October. The only exceptions are in Winnipeg Beach, Dunnottar and Victoria Beach, where elections were held July 24.
"It's a great day to go out and exercise your right to vote," said Sherwood Armbruster, the City of Winnipeg's senior election official.
Results for all of Manitoba will be updated as they are received from voting locations on the 2026 Manitoba municipal elections website shortly after polls close at 8 p.m., .
CBC Manitoba will also have coverage of the election online and on radio and television.
Voters wait in line at Bison Run School for the polling station to open on Wednesday morning. (Meaghan Ketcheson/CBC)
Tyler Wiwchar was first in line to cast his ballot at Bison Run School in the Waverley West neighbourhood of south Winnipeg, stopping on his way to work.

"I thought the first stop would be coming to vote as it it's an important thing to do — try to get there as soon as possible," he said. "Everyone should be able to have the opportunity to come vote and select someone that represents Winnipeg."
His choice was still being determined as he waited for the door to open. As Wiwchar did some last second research, he used a sports analogy for making a selection.
"Yeah, just like a hockey decision, a quick and quick and simple play," he joked.
Bola Osagie says she believes the people she voted for 'are good candidates that would move this area forward.' (Rudy Gauer/CBC)
Bola Osagie, who made her choice right after Wiwchar at Bison Run School, called it a privelege to vote.
“It's a wonderful opportunity to express what I wanna see done in the city," she said.
"I listened to them talk and I found out about the people I wanted to vote for and I believe that they are good candidates that would move this area forward."
The City of Winnipeg says the busiest times at polling stations are typically right when the they open and then again from 3 p.m. until close.
Don’t worry if you're still waiting to vote at the deadline, Armbruster said. As long as you're in line, you'll be able to mark your choices.

"If you are attending during a peak period, thank you for coming and being patient and getting to know your neighbours and know that we are providing the service as quickly and accurately as absolutely possible," he said.
If you have the option, consider voting during the quieter period between 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., when the process may be a little quicker.
Winnipeg voters must be Canadian citizens, at least 18 years old on Oct. 28 and Winnipeg residents or property owners for at least six months (since April 28), the city says.
Eligibility to vote in municipal and school board elections can by found on the provincial government website. This includes eligibility for non-resident voters in municipal elections.
More choice
More Manitobans are getting a choice of who leads their communities than in 2022.
There are fewer acclamations compared to four years ago, the Association of Manitoba Municipalities said. Uncontested races are down to 30 per cent from 37 per cent in 2022.
At the same time, the number of women candidates has increased to 340 this year from 289 in the previous election, the association said.
Incumbent mayors in several Manitoba communities, however, were acclaimed after no challengers registered to run. Those include Portage la Prairie, Winkler and Niverville.

items: More Manitobans get a choice of candidates in this year's municipal election

blocks.text: Some places, like the Municipality of Cartwright-Roblin and the Rural Municipality of Argyle, saw their entire slate of council candidates acclaimed.

There's also more voting flexibility this year in Winnipeg, home to more than half the province's population. There are 184 polling stations and registered voters should have received a card letting them know exactly when and where to cast a ballot.
"The voters card is going to present not one, but two convenient locations," said Armbruster.

"We're also proud of the fact that we had a record number of advanced voters. More than 50,000 Winnipeggers have already cast their vote, which is 20 per cent higher than the previous record that was set four years ago."

items: Winnipeg, Brandon set early vote record as advance polls close

blocks.text: If someone hasn’t received a voters card, they can call 311 to ask where their polling station is, or look it up on the city's where do I vote? web page.
"We always recommend you bring your voters notice if you have one. If you don't, bring one piece of valid government-issued photo ID with your name and current address," said Armbruster.
A list of accepted ID is available on the city's website.
If you're not sure which ward you live in, you can check out a series of ward maps on the City of Winnipeg website. There's a set of school division ward boundary maps too.
With files from Meaghan Ketcheson

articles.title: Russia in Africa: What is Putin hoping to achieve?
articles.summary: Following its invasion of Ukraine and the resulting rift with the West, Russia has declared that it intends to make a "historic return" to Africa. What have we seen of this so far?

image.caption: A poster in Burkina Faso depicts the country's military leader Ibrahim Traore with the Russian president Vladimir PutinImage: Christina Peters/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The conflict with the West sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine prompted Russian President Vladimir Putin to seek support from other parts of the world. Africa has become a focus, with foreign minister Sergei Lavrov visiting the continent increasingly often.
Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova has described it as a "historic return," and declared no one and nothing could be compared to what Russia did for Africa in the 20th century.
Russia's most important African partner: Egypt

A Russia-Africa summit has been held in Russia at roughly three-year intervals since 2019. The third takes place in Moscow on October 28 and 29. The program focusses on economic cooperation. Other topics range from politics and security to science and culture. But Russia is actively working with only a few African countries, mainly in the north of the continent, and this is reflected in the trade figures.

"South Africa is still Africa's largest national economy, but its volume of trade with Russia is small, far less than with Egypt and Algeria," says Ivan Klyszcz from the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Tallinn, Estonia.

"Egypt and Algeria in particular are key partners for Russia. Egypt plays an important role in this regard. Russian diplomats and business representatives are trying to extend relationships with other countries, especially Tanzania and Ethiopia, but with no appreciable success so far."

Egypt is the second-largest economy in Africa, and the bilateral volume of trade with Russia has more than doubled since 2021; in 2025, according to Russia's Federal Customs Service, it was $10.5 billion (€9.4 billion). Consignments of Russian grain are the main drivers, followed by products of the metal industry. Egypt's exports to Russia are primarily fruit and vegetables.

There are investment projects, too. Russia is building a big nuclear power plant in the Egyptian region of El-Dabaa on the Mediterranean coast. Construction is being financed by a Russian loan of 25 billion US dollars, which covers around 85% of the costs.

blocks.caption: Construction site of the Russian-financed El-Dabaa nuclear power plant in EgyptImage: SNA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Egypt is one of the few African countries with which Russia enjoys stable business relationships, as well as having extensive experience of cooperation, says Nikita Smagin, an expert on Russian policy in the Middle East. "In the long term, Egypt could become Moscow's gateway to Africa and to other markets," he says. "But Cairo is pursuing its own interests. It would be too optimistic to hope that Egypt is lending its support purely out of political solidarity."
Russia's economic role in Africa

According to the Russian customs service, around 39% of Russian–African trade in 2025 was with Egypt, and total sales between Russia and all 54 countries of the African continent came to around 27 billion US dollars. Africa's share of Russia's foreign trade is therefore very small (3.9% in 2025), and not at all commensurate with the attention Moscow is devoting to its relations with African countries.

Russia is not a significant trading partner for Africa, either. The most important partner for African countries is the European Union. In 2025, the volume of trade with the EU came to around 385 billion US dollars. African countries' statistics also show that other partners were well ahead of Russia. The volume of trade with China was in excess of 348 billion US dollars in 2025; with the United States it was almost 105 billion, and 103 billion with India.

Fidel Owusu, a Ghanaian expert with Geopolitical Intelligence Services (GIS) in Liechtenstein, comments that Russia's economic presence in Africa has not been as significant as that of China, the United States, India, or other traditional powers like France and Britain. "If you look at the volume of trade and the kind of investment," he says, "in recent times, some middle powers such as Turkey and the UAW are doing far better than Russia."

Beverly Ochieng, a senior analyst with Control Risks, a global risk and strategic intelligence consultancy in Senegal, observes: "Western countries continue to dominate in strategically important areas such as raw material extraction, finance, and the energy sector, even if their political presence in the region is declining." According to her, "Russia will compete more intensively for access to critical mineral resources and energy projects. We see this with lithium projects in Mali as well as with nuclear power initiatives across the continent."
Russian mercenaries in Africa

Russia's presence in Africa is more obvious in the military sector than in the fields of trade and investment. Starting with the arrival of the Wagner Group, Russian mercenaries have been supporting African regimes, particularly those of the unstable countries in the Sahel region. In exchange, their associated subsidiaries are granted access to raw materials. Following the death of the Wagner Group leader, Yevgeny Prigozhin, most of these operations were taken over by the Africa Corps, a paramilitary group set up and controlled by Russia's defense ministry.

According to the Congressional Research Service, the think tank of the US Congress, the largest Russian military contingents, each comprising several thousand men, are in the Central African Republic, Mali, and Libya. The Africa Corps is also keen to extend its presence in Burkina Faso and Niger. Russian mercenaries have also been spotted in Equatorial Guinea.
How Mali's big bet on Russia is backfiring

Irina Filatova from the University of Cape Town stresses that there are several reasons why it's important for Russia to maintain a military presence in Africa. "The countries have sizeable deposits of minerals such as gold and uranium. Through them, it's possible to exert influence over Europe's southern borders, including in matters of migration and regional security. With regard to Libya, the country is an important logistical hub for connections with the Sahel and central Africa. Goods can easily be supplied via Libya to countries without access to the sea," Filatova says.

Ultimately, Russia is still one of the biggest suppliers of arms to African countries, even though Russian exports have fallen over the course of the war in Ukraine. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates Moscow's share of the African market for the years 2021–2025 at 15%, which puts it in third place behind the United States (19%) and China (17%). Between 2020 and 2024, its share was even higher: It was in first place with 21%, followed by China with 18%, and the US with 16%.
What are Russia's diplomatic aims in Africa?

Ivan Klyszcz from the ICDS says that while Russia is not a significant economic partner for Africa, the fact that it supplies food and fertilizer and has a military presence in some countries means that Moscow's influence in Africa is far greater than is suggested by the volume of trade and investment alone.

"I believe Russia sees the diplomatic weight of Africa," says Fidel Owusu. "When I talk of diplomatic weight, I mean numbers – the continent has the largest number of countries. Russia wants that kind of support in the UN General Assembly whenever votes are cast. In recent times it has done better than in earlier votes."
The perception of Russia in Africa
In recent years, Russia has been positioning itself on the international stage as representing the interests of the Global South.

"We want to work with Africa, we are working with Africa and we will continue to do so. But our aim is not, as it was for the colonial powers, to make money or steal something from Africa, but to develop together," Russian president Vladimir Putin said recently at a conference of the Moscow-based Valdai Discussion Club.

blocks.caption: Russian president Vladimir Putin referred to the colonization of Africa by European powers and said Russia would do things differently Image: Mikhail Metzel/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: References to the colonial past appeal to some countries but not others, says Irina Filatova. "Africa is not a country, it's a continent. There are differences in the perception of Russia, as well as in the way Russia positions itself. Also, the views of the political elites are often substantially different from those of ordinary citizens. In South Africa, for instance, the Russian narrative is received very positively. An anti-colonial agenda is also popular in other countries, but it isn't necessarily associated with Russia."
Antonio Cascais contributed to this report. It was originally written in Russian.

articles.title: Bernardo on saying Jinggoy got P573 million in kickbacks: It's hard to implicate a friend
articles.summary: State witness Roberto Bernardo said it wasn"t easy for him to implicate Senator Jinggoy Estrada, whom he accused of receiving P573 million worth of “commitments” or kickbacks.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 5:46pm

State witness and former Public Works undersecretary Roberto Bernardo on Wednesday said it wasn’t easy for him to implicate Senator Jinggoy Estrada, whom he accused of receiving kickbacks from government projects.
Bernardo made the testimony when he was quizzed by Sandiganbayan Fifth Division justices and Estrada’s counsel, Laurence Arroyo, as to why he did not implicate Estrada in his September 2025.

Bernardo only later accused Estrada of receiving “commitments” of kickbacks from government infrastructure projects in November 2025 and in his latest October 26, 2026 judicial affidavit, which claimed the amount of kickbacks Estrada received reached P573 million.

“During that time [of my first affidavit], I have no confirmation, I have no solid evidence that will prove [his involvement]. I have already in [my] mind that he is a proponent [of projects], but I have to confirm [first],” Bernardo said.
“Ang hirap po ipahamak ang kaibigan. Hindi ko po agad magagawa iyon,” Bernardo added.
(It is tough to betray a friend. I cannot do that easily.)
Bernardo also pointed out that his previous affidavit, made prior to 2026, provides that given the complexities in the case, he reserved his right to “execute a supplemental affidavit if warranted.”
Bernardo also testified that the P573 million were delivered to Estrada in four installments: in November 2024, December 2024, February 2025, and June 2025.
Bernardo said he only personally delivered the commitments to Estrada in June 2025.
“It was June of 2025 when I delivered [it] with my driver,” he said.
“It was in multiples of P20 million [per sealed box] per report of Opulencia. Alam ko po na may ganoong halaga,” he said.
(I know that such is the amount.)
Gerard Opulencia is also a state witness like Bernardo and a former regional director of the Department of Public Works and Highways National Capital Region District Engineering Office.
Bernardo also said that Estrada asked for P1 billion project allocation under Senate leadership fund for election spending.
Bernardo told the anti-graft court what was indicated in his judicial affidavit wherein he said Estrada told him, “Tulungan mo na lang ako diyan kasi marami pa akong tutulungan sa eleksyon.”
(Kindly help me because I will be helping a lot of people during the 2025 elections).
Asked by the Sandiganbayan justices if the request was made in person, Bernardo said it was through a phone call.
“Tawag po,” Bernardo said.
When the court held a five-minute recess a few minutes after these statements by Bernardo, Estrada asked the Sandiganbayan to allow him to return to his cell in New Quezon City jail in Payatas.
Sought for comment, Estrada said he was satisfied with the cross-examination of his lawyers and that Bernardo’s testimony is inconsistent.
“Hindi naman siya nagdala ng pera sa akin,” Estrada said.
(He did not bring money to me.) — BM, GMA News
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot stake rival claims to lead Israel after deadlocked vote
articles.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot offered competing claims to lead Israel after Tuesday's election, with Netanyahu calling for a right-wing government and Eisenkot saying…

blocks.text: World·New

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot offered competing claims to lead Israel after Tuesday's election, with Netanyahu calling for a right-wing government and Eisenkot saying voters had rejected the longtime Israeli leader, even as early counting showed no clear winner.
Voter turnout was 77.7%, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than 2 decades
No clear winner in pivotal Israeli election, exit polls suggest

Israel's Central Elections Committee was tallying votes on Wednesday and it will likely take until Thursday before definitive results of the election — the first since the Hamas-led attack of Oct. 7, 2023 — are known.

With some 48.4 per cent of votes tallied, Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 55 seats, and Eisenkot's bloc 50 seats, with 15 seats going to Arab parties, Israeli media reported — a distribution will likely change as more votes are tallied.
That leaves both sides short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, and neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot claimed victory.

While the projected results may represent a setback for Netanyahu and his nationalist-religious coalition, a deadlock could work in his favour, leaving the 77-year-old in office as a caretaker prime minister during what are likely to be prolonged coalition negotiations or even until another election can be held.

An aide speaks to Likud Leader Benjamin Netanyahu as he gives a statement following exit polls for Israel's national election, at the party's election headquarters in Jerusalem early Wednesday. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

Netanyahu's bloc ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, which themselves campaigned on a platform of bringing down the prime minister and his far-right allies. Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party and a former military chief, has all but ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, complicating his path to power.
Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Netanyahu's bloc — with no major gains for either of them.

items: Israelis shatter turnout records in election that will pass wartime judgment on Netanyahu
Will Israeli voters turf Netanyahu?

blocks.text: Netanyahu, addressing party faithful after 3 a.m. local time at Likud election headquarters in Jerusalem, called for the formation of "a strong, right-wing national government."
Trump backed Netanyahu
He also highlighted Israel's military successes and raised the prospect of renewed joint action with U.S. President Donald Trump against Iran.

"Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all. But ulterior motives must not divert us from this sacred mission," he said.
Trump, who endorsed Netanyahu, was asked early on Wednesday about the election after a campaign trip to Texas, and said he did very well.
Supporters of Gadi Eisenkot react after the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election in Tel Aviv on Tuesday. (Ariel Schalit/The Associated Press)

"You know, it's pretty close, which was very well. Because I think when the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot, but I actually heard he did pretty well. It might be winning or tie. The tie is sort of considered a win in that case because it's a big chess match."
Eisenkot said the public had voted against Netanyahu remaining prime minister and urged him to retire from politics, while warning against the use of Israel's security for political purposes.
High voter turnout

"Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people's trust," Eisenkot said, calling on the security establishment to "stand firm" against any attempt to put political interests ahead of Israel's security.
Voter turnout was 77.7 per cent, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around seven percentage points higher than in 2022.

Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers in coalition negotiations that have run to weeks or months after past elections. If neither bloc can form a government, another vote may need to be held, something Eisenkot opposed given the high voter turnout.
No clear winner
If projections hold, Netanyahu's right-wing bloc, which at its height held 68 seats, would fall short of the 61 needed to govern, leaving him with no clear path to forming a government.

items: Netanyahu 'fighting for his political life' in 1st Israeli vote since Oct. 7. He might still survive
Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election

blocks.text: Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu's strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically.
He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticizing the prime minister's leadership.

A man walks past a Likud party campaign banner in Tel Aviv on Tuesday, featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump, with a Hebrew message reading, 'We have one opportunity to win.' (Baz Ratner/The Associated Press)

Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hawkish approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
Eisenkot says Israel's response — a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities — was a failure because Hamas remains in charge.

Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel's deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people, according to Israeli government tallies, and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran that followed.
While Netanyahu was criticized for the country's biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by killing top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

articles.title: Ten reported dead after two trains collide in Spain – Europe live
articles.summary:
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo

At least 10 people are feared dead and many more injured after two high-speed…

blocks.text: At least 10 feared dead after collision in Toledo province

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
At least 10 people are feared dead and many more injured after two high-speed trains collided in Toledo province in central Spain.

Spain’s state rail infrastructure authority said services between Madrid and the southern region of Andalucía had been suspended “⁠following a rear-end collision between two trains” on Wednesday morning.
A spokesperson for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha region, where the crash occurred, said the cause and ‌ number of injuries were yet to be determined.
Government sources told El País at least 10 people had been killed, and that the crash could be worse than the Adamuz rail disaster in January in which 46 people were killed.
We will bring you all updates here.
Key events

items: 15m agoDeath toll likely to rise, local government spokesperson warns
18m agoAt least 10 feared dead after collision in Toledo province

blocks.text: Today’s accident evokes grim echoes of last year’s tragedy in Adamuz, where 46 people killed and 152 were injured after two high-speed trains crashed in Adamuz, the province of Córdoba.

With almost 4,000km of track, Spain’s high-speed railway network ranks as the largest in Europe and the second biggest in the world after China, according to the Spanish infrastructure administrator Adif.

The network is tremendously popular, competitively priced and generally considered a safe mode of transport. In 2024, Renfe said more than 25 million passengers had travelled on its high-speed trains that year.

But in another major incident in 2013, 80 people died after a train derailed in the country’s north-west near Santiago de Compostela. An investigation concluded the train was travelling at 179km/h on a stretch of the line with an 80km/h speed limit when it left the tracks.
We are getting first pictures from the scene now…
Death toll likely to rise, local government spokesperson warns
Local government spokesperson told TVE that the death toll “will almost certainly rise.”
Esther Padilla told the broadcaster the situation “is going to worsen.”
She said the affected trains are likely to be Iryo 7076 with 146 passengers plus one baby on board, and AVE 2080 with 397 passengers on board, El País reported.

articles.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
articles.summary:
Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment

The “unprecedented”

blocks.text: The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.
“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

blocks.caption: Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa CDC. Photograph: Ken Cedeno/Reuters

blocks.text: Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”
This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.
France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

blocks.caption: Travellers at a hand-washing station in Busia on the Kenya-Uganda border, where health officials screen for Ebola symptoms, 12 October.  Photograph: Bright Emoja/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.
Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.
“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

blocks.caption: Red Cross staff simulate evacuating the remains of an Ebola victim in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, 22 October. Photograph: Tony Karumba/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

articles.title: Spain train crash: at least 10 feared dead after collision in Toledo province
articles.summary:
High-speed service reportedly runs into back of another train, knocking two carriages off track

At least 10 people are feared dead and many more injured after two high-speed trains…

blocks.text: At least 10 people have died and many more are feared injured after two high-speed trains collided in Toledo province in central Spain.

Spain’s state rail infrastructure authority said services between Madrid and the southern region of Andalucía had been suspended “⁠following a rear-end collision between two trains” on Wednesday morning.

Esther Padilla, a spokesperson for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha region, where the crash occurred, said authorities could confirm 10 deaths. “The information we are receiving is not good at all. There are at least 10 dead and it is possible that the number will increase,” Padilla told local media.
Government sources told El País that the crash could be worse than the Adamuz rail disaster in January in which 46 people were killed.

blocks.caption: Passengers check departure boards at Santa Justa station in Seville after the crash. Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty Images

blocks.text: Spain’s state broadcaster, TVE, reported that the crash happened after a high-speed train ran into the back of another service, knocking two carriages off the track.

Footage broadcast by regional Castilla La Mancha Television ​showed a derailed train with at least one carriage remaining on an elevated section of track. Twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line.
The rail operator Adif said the collision occurred on ⁠the line from Madrid to Seville.
Manuel Galán, the mayor ​of ​Urda near the ​city of Toledo, said he had ​been ‌asked by ​emergency ​services to prepare a sports hall to accommodate the injured.
Spain’s main political parties, which are gearing up for next month’s general election, suspended their planned activities for the day.

The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, expressed his shock at news of the crash. “I remain in constant contact with the transport minister, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha,” he said in a post on X. “Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My love, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families.”

The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said on X: “Very concerned about the information we are getting about a new rail accident. The priority now is to attend to the victims and support their families. My full support to the emergency teams working on the ground.”
