articles.title: Record amounts of Canadian cannabis seized as smuggling to Europe soars
articles.summary: Legalization of cannabis in Canada is having unintended and serious consequences an ocean away. Belgian customs seized 21 tonnes of Canadian cannabis in 2025 alone, exceeding illegal exports from…
articles.byline: Nahlah Ayed, Brenda Witmer, Charlotte Wirth

image.caption: This photo provided by Belgian customs shows a container from Canada, containing wooden fire briquettes, which arrived at the port of Antwerp in February. When customs opened the container, they found one-kilogram vacuum-sealed bags of Canadian cannabis hidden in crates within the shipment. (Belgian

blocks.text: Hidden in a shipping container full of a family's household belongings. Stashed in crates cleverly built inside a facade of wooden fire briquettes. All neatly vacuum packed and labelled, and then shipped across the ocean.
Nearly a decade after it was legalized at home, Canadian-grown marijuana is being smuggled through Europe's largest ports, leading to record seizures and a call for Canadian officials to intervene.

According to Belgian customs officials, a record-breaking 21 tonnes of Canadian cannabis were seized in the port of Antwerp in 2025 alone, exceeding illegal exports from every other country in the world. That includes Morocco, until recently Europe's biggest supplier of illicit weed.

Officials told CBC News that smugglers are taking full advantage of Canada's decision in 2018 to legalize cannabis use to illegally ship it across the world and tap into the highly profitable European market. Criminals stand to make many more times in returns in Europe than what the same marijuana fetches at home.

"According to my information, it has to do with the policy of the Canadian government," Kristian Vanderwaeren, director general of the Belgian Customs and Excise, told CBC News in an interview in Brussels.
"And 320 million Europeans who have money to buy this … it's an immense market."

Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, says the average wholesale price of a kilo of Canadian marijuana in a place like the Netherlands (where marijuana use is decriminalized, but technically illegal, as it is all over Europe) is about 4,100 Euros ($6,429 Cdn), and as much as 6,000 Euros (about $9,408 Cdn) in the U.K. Street prices would be even higher.
Kristian Vanderwaeren, director general of the Belgian Customs and Excise, says criminal organizations either earn a lot of money through smuggling or they don’t do it. (David Iacolucci/CBC)
In Canada, the wholesale price for a kilogram of dried cannabis is an average of $1,000 to $1,500 Cdn, according to the RCMP.

Vanderwaeren says he first noted the surge in 2024, and then seizures at the port spiked in 2025, prompting a "red alert." That’s when he contacted the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) for help in stemming the tide.
The port of Rotterdam, the largest in Europe, is also experiencing a surge in Canadian cannabis seizures this year.

CBSA confirmed intelligence indicates "a sustained increase in illegal export attempts since 2022, particularly to Europe" including Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, France and others. In an emailed response to CBC’s questions, a spokesperson for the agency said such attempts are done "in cargo shipments, postal shipments, and smuggling by air passengers."
In 2025 alone, CBSA says its agents seized about 34 tonnes of cannabis products intended for export at maritime border points.
Still, Canada's policy is having a palpable impact in Europe, says Belgium's first-ever drug commissioner.
"This cannabis is sold in our Belgian streets but it's also going to the rest of Europe," said Ine Van Wymersch.
"This is a supply-driven market," she added.
"We see that criminal groups are taking advantage of a gray zone, that it is really hard for the Canadian government to mitigate and to regulate this whole new policy."
Legalization policies "sound very good in theory, but we have to take into account human behaviour," she said.
Belgian drug commissioner Ine Van Wymersch says information needs to be exchanged on both sides of the ocean to stop the smuggling. (David Iacolucci/CBC)

Van Wymersch, once Belgium's youngest public prosecutor, was appointed drug commissioner in 2023 to aid in the fight against rising drug crime. Brussels alone has seen a significant surge — 74 shootings so far this year, according to the Brussels-Capital region’s minister-president.
"The shootings we see and the explosions are overall mainly related to cocaine but also to cannabis," said Van Wymersch.

The violence has prompted a debate on whether Belgium may be devolving into a "narco state." Van Wymersch rejects that label, but in one indication of the severity of the situation, she is always protected by a security team.
"We can't be naive," she said. "These criminal gangs, they don't have any values.” To do her job, “there are some measures that need to be taken to protect me and my office."
Although drugs are also smuggled through Belgium's airports, most come via the port of Antwerp, officially called Antwerp-Bruges. It has long been considered a top cocaine gateway to Europe.
Smugglers are now using the same maritime lines, well-established criminal networks and logistics through Antwerp and Rotterdam to get Canadian marijuana to Europe, says Europol.
A drug sniffing dog searches a container during a customs control for drugs at the Belgian port of Antwerp-Bruges, on May 20, 2022. (Valeria Mongelli/AFP/Getty Images)

Europol gave CBC News exclusive insights on the movement of Canadian cannabis, including how criminal networks react when they encounter obstacles: "[They] will adjust, for example, by routing containers from Canada via the U.S. It is possible that cannabis from Canada destined for Europe could transit via the Caribbean."
"Smuggling is like surfing," said Vanderwaeren, the chief of customs. "You have to find the wave."

items: Toronto man charged after disguising cannabis as frozen waffles while entering U.S., officials say
Hamilton man pleads guilty to smuggling marijuana into U.S. via helicopter

blocks.text: In other words, the criminal networks are swiftly adapting.
The surge in supply from Canada has meant Belgian seizures of marijuana at the port of Antwerp have for the first time overtaken those of cocaine.

CBC News is the first Canadian media organization to gain access to customs inspections at Antwerp, as well as a glimpse into some of the inventive ways smugglers tried to get Canadian cannabis through.
'Something was off'

One case concerned a container that arrived from Canada last February, ostensibly filled with the belongings of a family moving to France. Agents became suspicious when they spotted two juke boxes whose electrical innards had been removed, stashed among innocuous-looking household goods.
Once they opened the container, agents found packages of marijuana stacked inside the hollowed-out juke boxes.
Agents inspecting X-ray-like images of another container noticed an anomaly: What was supposed to be pallets-full of wooden briquettes for fires appeared darker at the edges.

This image supplied by Belgian customs shows juke boxes that had been stripped of all electronics and stuffed with Canadian cannabis. The machines were hidden in a container full of belongings from people who were moving from Canada to France. It arrived at the port of Antwerp in February. (Belgian Customs and Excise)
"My colleagues could see something was off," said communications officer Sara Van Cotthem.
They discovered that the briquettes were in fact a facade hiding crates that held vacuum-packed, one kilogram pouches of cannabis.

The port sees the equivalent of 13.5 million, 20-foot containers a year. Only one to two per cent of those containers are inspected, says Van Cotthem, using tools ranging from dogs, to scanners, to artificial intelligence and plain old intuition.
The rise in Canadian cannabis seizures has meant more scrutiny for Canadian containers than before, said Van Cotthem.
Sara Van Cotthem, a communications officer with Belgian customs, says officers undergo intensive training to learn how to spot suspicious shipments. (Brenda Witmer/CBC)
Any seized drugs are ultimately incinerated, she added. Finding the culprits is left to law enforcement in Europe and in Canada.

A recent example was a trial in Berlin that convicted ten men for smuggling marijuana from Canada to Germany, handing the three main defendants sentences ranging from six and a half to 15 years in prison. The judge ruled the three used a front company to move 1.1 tonnes of cannabis in shipping containers ostensibly carrying timber.
'Glocal' problem

Vanderwaeren says that since his appeal to Canada, he's noted a slight decrease in marijuana seizures in recent months, though the overall numbers remain high. He credits the CBSA’s ramped up efforts.
A letter of intent was subsequently signed between the heads of customs of Canada, Belgium, as well as France and The Netherlands, to cooperate on stymying smugglers.

However, Europol says the profitability of North American cannabis (due to its high potency and low production cost) coupled with the demand in Europe, "ensures that this illicit trade will likely persist and even grow." The profits will help fund other criminal activities, the agency added.

The CBSA says the RCMP is "aware of sophisticated transnational organized crime groups involved in the illegal cannabis market, including networks engaged in both illicit domestic distribution and international exportation."

The spokesperson added that Canada respects its obligations under international drug control treaties, and that the Cannabis Act regulates restrictions on import and export of cannabis. "Any other cannabis imports or exports … are prohibited."

items: RCMP charge 2 men for allegedly using women to smuggle cannabis from Toronto to Nigeria
Air Canada employee charged after alleged weed smuggling scheme at Pearson airport

blocks.text: Belgian officials are at pains to say they are not blaming Canada. But Vanderwaeren says that Canadians need to be aware of the unintended consequences of policies that are effectively "sponsoring criminal organizations" by enabling their huge profits.
Van Wymersch agreed, describing drug smuggling as a "glocal" problem — combining local and global — and so the solutions must be too.

"It will not help us to blame each other. Because we need each other," she said. "If we don't focus on the global level and we don't act on the local level, we will never come to something sustainable."

articles.title: Why the Hispanic vote could sway the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections
articles.summary: While millions of U.S. voters have become only more entrenched in their party loyalties in the era of Donald Trump, the large and growing Hispanic community has instead bucked that partisan trend. A…

image.caption: Supporters of Bobby Pulido, the Democratic Party candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in a South Texas district, stationed outside a polling station in Edinburg, Texas, during early voting for the U.S. midterm elections. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New

While millions of U.S. voters have become only more entrenched in their party loyalties in the era of Donald Trump, the large and growing Hispanic community has instead bucked that partisan trend. A willingness to cast ballots across party lines has made the roughly 39 million Hispanic eligible voters a crucial demographic at election time, courted equally by Democrats and Republicans.
Hispanic voters have soured on Republicans over ICE and economy — but many don't vote along party lines
While millions of U.S. voters have become only more entrenched in their party loyalties in the era of Donald Trump, the large and growing Hispanic community has instead bucked that partisan trend.

A willingness to cast ballots across party lines has made the roughly 39 million Hispanic eligible voters in the U.S. a crucial demographic at election time, courted equally by Democrats and Republicans.
They swung toward Trump in record numbers in 2024.

But if their current dissatisfaction with Trump's performance as president translates into votes in next Tuesday's midterms, the Latino community could potentially sway some crucial races and tip the balance of power in Congress toward the Democrats.

Latinos are the "swingiest" voters in the nation, says Javier Palomarez, president and CEO of the U.S. Hispanic Business Council, which advocates for the 4.5 million Hispanic-owned companies (small and large) across the country.

"We are a community that doesn't vote party, it votes person," Palomarez told CBC News. "You'll see Republicans willing to vote for a Democrat in the Hispanic community very often, and conversely Democrats willing to go for a Republican."

U.S. President Donald Trump travelled to Corpus Christi, Texas, for a campaign rally on Tuesday to try to boost support for Republican midterm candidates in the largely Hispanic districts of south Texas. (Eric Vryn/The Associated Press)
Trump increased his share of Hispanic voters in each successive election since 2016, garnering the highest percentage ever for a Republican presidential candidate in 2024, according to exit polls.
Yet the very issues that drove Hispanic support for Trump in 2024 — reducing the cost of living and tightening border security — could be the ones that hurt the Republicans in the 2026 midterms.
ICE tactics draw fire
Some Hispanic voters are focused on how Trump's decision to go to war with Iran triggered a sharp rise in the price of gas and diesel across the U.S.

Others are deeply concerned by the way Trump dramatically ramped up detention of undocumented Hispanics who've lived upstanding lives in the U.S. for years, rather than sticking to his pledge of deporting violent criminals.

items: How Canada and tariffs are factoring into U.S. midterm elections

blocks.text: In Texas, where Hispanics make up roughly one-third of eligible voters, disenchantment with Trump and the Republicans is palpable in the Latino-majority cities of the Rio Grande Valley.

CBC News shadowed a team of get-out-the-vote canvassers for LUPE Votes — an activist group whose name, La Unión del Pueblo Entero, translates as "union of all the people" — in the border city of Edinburg.

Canvassers with the activist group LUPE Votes prepare to knock on doors in the predominantly Hispanic city of Edinburg, Texas, with early voting under way in the U.S. midterms. José Ferrer, right, says his stepfather was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and later deported. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

One of the canvassers, 24-year-old Jose Ferrer, said his stepfather was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Father's Day this year. The family found his truck abandoned at the side of the road and didn't hear from him for two weeks. He was deported to Mexico two months later.

"I'm not the only one getting affected, obviously," Ferrer told CBC News. His mother-in-law, a teacher, has described her students' parents being grabbed by ICE agents while waiting for the school bus.
ICE enforcement 'brutal' in south Texas: developer
The anger in the community over ICE tactics cuts across economic lines.

Mario Guerrero, a developer who voted for Trump three times because he considered him a very successful businessman, says immigration enforcement is one of the key reasons he'll vote Democrat on the midterm ballot.
"I believe in the American dream," Guerrero said in an interview at the site of a supermarket he's building beside a new housing development in Pharr, next door to Edinburg.

"The ICE enforcement that we've been seeing here in south Texas has been brutal," he said, adding that the job-site and roadside raids have scared off so many people from coming to work that the pace of construction projects slowed to a crawl.
Mario Guerrero, CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, oversees work on a grocery store his company is building on the edge of a residential subdivision in Pharr, Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
"All of our workers are documented," Guerrero said. "The problem is [ICE agents are] apprehending, they're taking people with the proper documentation."
He believes the tactics will have midterm consequences for the Republicans, including "a turnout of Mexican Americans like they've never seen before."
Hispanic voting bloc defies generalization
Hispanic people now account for one-sixth of the eligible voters in the U.S., a larger group than Black Americans, according to data compiled by Pew Research Center.

But they defy broad generalizations as a voting bloc. They encompass devout Catholics, fiscally conservative entrepreneurs, working class immigrants-turned-citizens and college-educated Hispanics whose families have been in the U.S. for generations.

items: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency

blocks.text: "We have seen over and over with data that we cannot put Latino voters in one category," said Dayana Iza, Texas director of Mi Familia Vota, a national organization that aims to build Latino political power.
She describes the group's work as helping Hispanic Americans "connect the dots" to understand how elections can have a tangible impact on their daily lives.
Álvaro Corral, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, specializes in the politics of Latino voters in the U.S. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
"That is what is really going to make a difference with how Latinos turn out for these midterms," Iza told CBC News.
"There are a lot of Latinos that still do not participate in this electoral process, and those are the folks that we're really trying to target."
Nuance on immigration, border security
But even if there is a notable shift away from the Republicans at the midterms, it won't necessarily mean that Hispanic voters are fully embracing everything about the Democratic Party.

Neither party has accurately reflected the nuanced position of the typical Hispanic voter on immigration and border security, says Álvaro Corral, political science professor at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.
He says that position combines strong measures to keep criminals from flowing across the border with a pathway to citizenship for undocumented migrants who've long worked in the U.S.
Instead, the Trump administration's approach "is really offending the sensibilities and morality of a large portion of the Latino voters," Corral told CBC News.
Palomarez, of the U.S Hispanic Business Council, says the Democrats "took the Hispanic vote for granted" and at the national level shifted "a bit too left for the Hispanic community's liking."
That leeriness about the Democrats can be seen in the campaigns of some of their own Hispanic candidates.
Bobby Pulido, left, campaigning recently at a seniors' activity center in McAllen, Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
'Not Team Red. Not Team Blue'

Bobby Pulido, the Latino recording star who's trying to unseat incumbent Republican Monica De La Cruz in the 15th congressional district of Texas, downplays his party in his campaign ads and material.
"Not Team Red. Not Team Blue. Team You," says a slogan on the T-shirts worn by Pulido's campaign workers.

items: How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign
Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump

blocks.text: "Hispanics, they're not so partisan. It's very much, 'Are you gonna go fight for me?' That's what matters," Pulido told CBC News in an interview after he campaigned at a seniors' activity centre.
Still, Pulido says Hispanic Americans will punish Republican candidates in the midterms because they hate how ICE raids both separate families and disrupt the economy.
"When you add those two things, it's a very, very big explosion and you're going to see this Nov. 3."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: Queen of Canada documentary director wants you to know her followers are still out there
articles.summary: CBC News spoke with Queen of Canada director Cristian Gomes and journalist Mack Lamoureux about their new documentary, and why it focuses on Romana Didulo's past followers.

image.caption: Romana Didulo, holding a bullhorn, at a rally at Parliament Hill in Ottawa. She is the subject of a new Passionate Eye documentary. (Fathom Film Group)

blocks.text: Entertainment·INTERVIEW
CBC News spoke with Queen of Canada director Cristian Gomes and journalist Mack Lamoureux about their new documentary, and why it focuses on Romana Didulo's past followers.
Director Cristian Gomes, journalist Mack Lamoureux on why their new documentary focuses on Romana's followers
A little over a year ago, the RCMP raided a purple schoolhouse in Saskatchewan that had been taken over by a woman known as the "QAnon Queen of Canada."

It was the fallout of a movement years in the making: a group now widely referred to as a cult led by Romana Didulo — a self-described shapeshifting alien who passed her own "laws" in her self-described "Kingdom of Canada."
That group has largely disbanded, but its past members remain. They are the subjects of a new documentary, Queen of Canada, airing on CBC's The Passionate Eye on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

Because while the documentary does focus on Didulo's actions, she does not feature as an interview subject. Instead, director Cristian Gomes centres on those past followers, who both grapple with what they went through but who — in some cases — continue to believe in what they were working toward.
CBC News speaks with Gomes and subject Mack Lamoureux, the first journalist to seriously investigate and report on Didulo, about why that is so important.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
New doc Queen of Canada takes on Romana Didulo story

You speak to a number of people who followed Romana. They have since left her, but — as is shown in the documentary — they haven't given up many of their distrustful beliefs around the media and government. Was it hard to get them to talk to you?

Cristian Gomes: It was difficult to find the voices, only because I'm not a part of the ecosystem that they thrive in. But once you join them, once you figure out how to find their voice and engage with them online — like in places like Telegram and other really private chats — it isn't really hard to get them to talk.

It was a big learning lesson for me, as well. People to whose beliefs, at one point, I responded like 'These views are kind of abhorrent. They're really damaging, and they leak into all facets of society, actually.' But at the same time, they're human too. They're just people who are really lost and they're being taken advantage of.
Mack, I'm curious whether your interpretation might fall in line with Cristian's. Do you see this as a wider case study, one that illustrates that widening division within society?

Mack Lamoureux: I like to consider Romana a harbinger. I consider her a glimpse into a possible future that we're not necessarily tied to, but if we don't course-correct we could end up in that way. The disconnect from reality and the damage that her followers had was so extreme — and in many ways scary — that I do think that it's something that we need to try and take steps to fix.

The future looks bleak for a lot of people. On top of that, you have algorithms which are pushing people down these rabbit holes. You have influencers and media organizations who are all too happy to run with conspiracies if it means that they're going to strengthen their bottom dollar.

All of this adds into a toxic cocktail that can lead people to joining and following people like Romana and completely ruining their lives. The worse life gets for people, the more people are going to find their ways into the arms of bad actors like Romana.
Cult leader Romana Didulo set up a base in a decommissioned school in Richmound, Sask., in 2023. (CBC News)

The moment that stands out to me is when one of your interview subjects says she once told her adult son if he got the COVID-19 vaccine, she would kill herself. Speaking with you now, it does seem like this could be framed as, 'She feels so isolated, so ignored, that's why she felt she needed to make that statement.' Was that what you were going for?

CG: What is fascinating in the film is that the people who are making these statements have been through the process of a radicalization: being a part of a group, and then being disgruntled within that group and leaving it. And they still hold their views. And I think that really speaks to how deeply, deeply pushed to the fringes these people are.
They really have been totally put outside of the systems of politics in this country, and any other way they could express themselves. They have no outlet.

The dynamic between the character you're speaking about and her son is really interesting because her son, although he doesn't agree with all of her views, he found out how to have a relationship with her. And that's a big part of why she was able to leave the group.
That happens a lot in high-control groups; having someone on the outside who's just there to listen to you without judgment is what helps a lot of people leave.

items: Crown stays charges against self-proclaimed ‘Queen of Canada’
Saskatchewan mayor stepping down now that 'Queen of Canada' cult is gone

blocks.text: Mack, you've reported on cults and terrorist groups for years. How does healing work in that situation? Is there a way to fix this from a societal standpoint?

ML: For a lot of people, healing isn't a linear path, it's kind of hopping back and forth through these different things. And for a lot of these people, they're just not going to come back from it. And I think we need to be relatively OK with it. I think it's more about getting those folks to be a bit more of a functioning member of society than it is about trying to force them to believe our collective reality that we have.

I don't think there is a 'fixing it,' because I think it's an integral flaw in our design. But I do think that there are ways of making it better, because the technology that we have is accelerating it. But I don't think there is a world where we all hold hands and everything's fine. I wish I was a utopian, but…

items: Fjord's Sebastian Stan, Cristian Mungiu on making a movie no one can agree on
Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'

blocks.text: From your experience speaking with this group, Cristian, how has your interpretation changed? Is there a way to fix this situation, or will those who feel this ignored and separated continue to feel that way?
CG: A big part of this is people feeling like they have no voice. That's how they get ostracized. We all experience what it was like in COVID. We all experienced the polarization of it.

Something we have to realize is that there's this large group of Canadians who are very disenfranchised, who have been for a long time. They don't believe in political systems. Some of them don't even believe they're a part of Canada. They think they're in another sovereign state — that's how far they feel isolated from us.
And so when we see that happening and if we can acknowledge that's happening, we have to reach out to those people. We have to bring them back into the fold. We have to have conversations with them.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 10 students suspended at Lévis, Que., high school for posting AI-altered images of staff
articles.summary: Ten students at a high school in Lévis, Que., have been suspended after several AI-altered images of teachers and school staff were posted to Snapchat. Experts say both teachers and students need…

image.caption: Ten students were suspended at Horizon high school in Lévis, Que., after they posted AI-altered images of teachers and school staff on social media. (Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal

Ten students at a high school in Lévis, Que., have been suspended after several AI-altered images of teachers and school staff were posted to Snapchat. Experts say both teachers and students need more education about the risks of AI and online images.
Edited image on Snapchat reportedly showed gun being held to teacher's head
Ten students have been suspended at a high school in Lévis, Que., after images of teachers and school staff altered by artificial intelligence were published on social media.

In a statement, the school service centre, the Centre de services scolaire des Navigateurs (CSSDN), said the students at Horizon high school were suspended for violating the school’s code of conduct, which prohibits posting any "offensive, defamatory, hateful, or violent content or images."
It also forbids recording or broadcasting individuals without consent.

André Bernier, president of the Association québécoise du personnel de direction des écoles, a provincial group representing school administrators, told Radio-Canada most of the images in this case could be described as silly or nonsense.
But Bernier said he was told by the school that one of the fake images posted on Snapchat reportedly showed a gun being held to the head of a teacher.
"Using photos without authorization is simply not tolerable — you never know where things might lead — so the school chose to intervene quickly in this matter," Bernier said.

The local school service centre the Centre de services scolaire des Navigateurs said in a statement it was other students who first alerted staff to the AI-doctored photos. (Philippe Kirouac/Radio-Canada)
The CSSDN said it was other students who first reported the images to school staff because they felt uncomfortable.
Administrators and the school's police officer met with the students who posted the images and asked them to delete them, which they agreed to do.
The students were suspended for three days, but no criminal charges were laid.
AI presents new risk

Richard Bergevin, president of the province's federation of teachers' unions, the Fédération des syndicats de l'enseignement (FSE-CSQ), said it’s important that schools take these situations seriously.
"When these photos and videos appear on the internet, they can have a very wide distribution," Bergevin said.
"Unfortunately, they can unfairly damage the reputation of a teacher," he said.
He said before Quebec instituted a ban on cellphones in schools, there were some incidents of students filming teachers in the classroom.
"They were making short videos to try and make teachers look bad, videos that were shared without any context," Bergevin said.
"With the ban on cellphones, these phenomena have decreased significantly in recent years, and teachers were less fearful," he said.

items: 1 year post cellphone ban in Quebec schools, here's how these students are adjusting

blocks.text: He said incidents such as this one with AI are more rare, but are presenting a new risk.
"With the power of the tools that artificial intelligence puts in the hands of students, these situations can occur more and more frequently," he said.
Bergevin said with AI, students can easily manipulate existing images and videos of teachers or school staff already posted online.
He said school administrators and school boards should sanction students, but also report such incidents to police when necessary.
André Bernier, president of an association representing school administrators, said students posting any photos of staff without their consent is unacceptable. (Pierre-Alexandre Bolduc/Radio-Canada)
Bernier said school staff also have to be careful about posting even innocuous images of school activities online that could be manipulated.
"There might be some training for staff to put in necessary blocks so people who are not part of their network won’t be able to use photos," Bernier said.
"It's always important to pay attention to the parameters, because when you're not careful, it becomes public and anyone can access it."
Teens need limits, guidance

Carolanne Campeau is a lecturer and a PhD student at University of Sherbrooke who’s also an adviser for a group called PAUSE, which provides support and creates awareness campaigns to address hyperconnectivity.
She said AI tools are largely unregulated and easy to access online.
"They are so easily available to kids. The government needs to regulate the platforms," Campeau said.
Behavioural addiction expert Carolanne Campeau says governments need to do more to regulate AI use for children. (Isaac Olson/CBC)
"I'm kind of flabbergasted that they can't come up with something that is more safe to use for our teenagers. It doesn’t make sense," she said.
Campeau said technology often moves more quickly than governments and the education system when it comes to drafting laws and regulations.
"Right now, the conversation is all about social media, and not necessarily AI," she said.
She thinks a moratorium on AI use for children under a certain age would be a good idea.

items: Why parents worry about their kids using AI in school

blocks.text: "We need to delay the introduction of these AI tools into their lives," Campeau said.
She believes young children shouldn't have access to AI tools at all, but that they could potentially be introduced to teenagers, accompanied by a robust digital literacy program in schools.
"We have to do it in a way that explains what the risks are, because the technology is not necessarily going to have those guardrails," Campeau said.

items: High school west of Montreal boosts security as it struggles with student fights, unrest

blocks.text: "We want them to have this critical thinking skill about what's possible, but also what is morally reprehensible, and what can actually lead to legal consequences," she said.
In a statement, new Education Minister Joël Arseneau said the school was right to suspend the students.
"We must act swiftly and decisively to send the message that there is zero tolerance throughout the school system for manipulations like those that occurred at Horizon high school," Arseneau said.
He said regulating AI in schools is a priority for the government, and that he was confident they would quickly find a way to prevent these types of situations from recurring.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Steve Rukavina has been with CBC News in Montreal since 2002. In 2019, he won a RTDNA award for continuing coverage of sexual misconduct allegations at Concordia University. He's also a co-creator of the podcast, Montreapolis. Before working in Montreal he worked as a reporter for CBC in Regina and Saskatoon. You can reach him at stephen.j.rukavina@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
articles.summary: The Villa Vie Odyssey suspended its voyage and is working with passengers on "temporary living arrangements".

blocks.text: A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.
The US-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800.

The company said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for scam centres.
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.
The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.
"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," one passenger, Holly Hennessey, told the BBC from Cambodia.
"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."
The Villa Vie Odyssey is equipped with several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website.
Permanent residencies in its cabins range from $120,000 to $440,000. These cabins are also also available for rent from $3,500 a month.
Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea.

In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package. Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election".

Hennessey said the ship's residents had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed". Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.
But some, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Villa Vie Odyssey will set sail again soon.
"Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said.
"Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out."

articles.title: Goodbye, SPNEC: MVP rebrands Leviste’s solar firm, lines up P5-B deal
articles.summary: A new name, five more solar businesses, and a possible "re-IPO," but Meralco's makeover can't quite banish Leviste's past or the P10.34-billion headache that comes with it

blocks.text: A new name, five more solar businesses, and a possible "re-IPO," but Meralco's makeover can't quite banish Leviste's past or the P10.34-billion headache that comes with it

items: Manuel V. Pangilinan is rebranding SP New Energy Corporation (SPNEC) to MGEN Renewables Inc. (MGENR) and integrating nearly P5 billion worth of renewable energy businesses.

The rebranding is part of a broader strategy by the Meralco group, distancing from the controversial past of Leandro Leviste's Solar Philippines, which faced contract terminations and financial obligations.
MGEN Renewables plans to strengthen its position by acquiring stakes in five solar businesses and is considering a 're-IPO' in March 2027, with expectations of improved financial performance.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Manuel V. Pangilinan is giving Leandro Leviste’s old solar crown jewel quite the makeover. First, shed the SPNEC name. Next, bring in nearly P5 billion worth of other renewable energy businesses.
And perhaps, pitch the shiny new thing to stock market investors all over again.

SP New Energy Corporation (SPNEC) is now officially MGEN Renewables Inc., (MGENR) after securing Securities and Exchange Commission approval on Monday, October 26; its stock ticker is also set to change to MGENR.

Officially, the renaming is part of the Meralco group’s broader rebranding strategy. Conveniently, it also removes a reminder of Solar Philippines, the controversial empire Leviste built before Pangilinan’s group took control.
And there’s quite a history behind SPNEC.

blocks.caption: FROM SPNEC to MGENR. This Rappler diagram shows the ownership of the rebranded solar company as of September 1, 2026 and before the proposed share swap. Diagram by Raphael Reyes/Rappler.

blocks.text: Leviste made his fortune assembling landholdings and securing solar development rights that attracted deep-pocketed investors, including Pangilinan himself. Industry sources that Rappler spoke with describe the young billionaire as a talented “flipper.”
But getting the rights to build solar farms and actually getting them built are two different businesses.

The Department of Energy (DOE) terminated 33 contracts tied to Leviste’s wider Solar Philippines group, covering around 11,400 megawatts of proposed capacity, and sought around P24 billion in financial obligations. His camp disputes the claims.
While much of the P24-billion mess relates to Leviste’s other companies, SPNEC is dragged into this too.
In a December 23, 2025 letter seen by Rappler, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin terminated the service contract for SPNEC’s 280-megawatt Santa Rosa Nueva Ecija 2 project and demanded P10.34 billion.

The DOE cited missed work-program commitments, an unrenewed performance bond, and missing documents, including a feasibility study and proof of land rights. Most of the demand came from P12.38 billion in work-program commitments, less P2.04 billion credited for reported accomplishments.

MGEN insists SPNEC is legally separate from Solar Philippines and not liable for the wider group’s P24 billion obligation. But it acknowledges that Santa Rosa belongs to SPNEC and says that it invoked force majeure over transmission delays and sought reconsideration.
Separately, Leviste and his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, face graft and plunder complaints involving solar contracts awarded to Leviste-linked companies. Both deny wrongdoing.

Leviste himself has kept his distance from his now Meralco-controlled company, resigning from the board in January and cashing out P3-billion worth of shares, leaving his holding company with an 11.51% stake.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] As Leandro Leviste cashes out of SPNEC, his private companies remain at the table

blocks.text: So, what’s next for MGENR?

On Tuesday, October 27, MGEN Renewables’ board approved a proposed P4.98-billion deal to take in stakes in five solar businesses from its controlling shareholder, MGEN Renewable Energy Inc., another Meralco subsidiary.
The companies have interests in operating solar plants across Luzon:

items: Greenergy for Global Inc. – 52.7-megawatt solar plant in Isabela
Greentech Solar Energy Inc. – 19.8-megawatt solar plant in Nueva Ecija
CACI Power Corporation – Linked to an 80.1-megawatt solar plant in Rizal
Nuevo Solar Energy Corporation – 68.7-megawatt solar plant in Ilocos Norte
PowerSource First Bulacan Solar Inc. – 55-megawatt solar plant in Bulacan

blocks.text: Instead of paying cash, MGEN Renewables will issue around 3.1 billion new shares to its controlling shareholder. If completed, the share swap deal would strengthen Meralco’s control while further diluting Leviste and other investors.
Then comes the more intriguing possibility, a “re-IPO” targeted for March 2027.
Since Leviste already took SPNEC public in 2021, this would be another share offering in the now bigger company under Meralco’s control, rather than a second listing. Nothing has been finalized.

This time, there’s more to show investors. Its P200-billion MTerra Solar project began commercial operations in August, while MGEN Renewables forecasts P774 million in profit for 2026, reversing a P4.1-billion loss in 2025.
The group also plans to invest up to another P7.815 billion in Terra Solar, subject to lender and investor approvals. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brings #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during the public forum to define what a liveable city should be

items: Rappler's MovePH hosted the #MoveCebu forum at the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 participants to discuss what makes a city livable.

Last week, Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brought #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during a public forum to define what a liveable city should be.

To solidify our long-term commitment to campus journalism and civic engagement, we proudly signed memoranda of understanding with the University of San Carlos, and the University of the Philippines Cebu.

Rappler multimedia reporter John Sitchon, who reports on Cebu and the Visayas region, joined us as we worked directly with participants. You can check out these stories to read more about what happened during the roadshow:

items: Padayon Cebu: A new space to chat how to make the province more livable
At #MoveCebu forum, Cebuanos define what a liveable city should be
MovePH trains Movers in Cebu on local reporting, civic organizing

blocks.text: Taking advantage of the momentum generated by the forum, we dove into focused workshops with 35 newly-trained Movers, and leaders from Cebu’s civil society groups to bridge reporting with civic organizing.
Our Movers who chose the civic mobilization track pitched bold, ground-level initiatives tackling community realities across Cebu province.

For example, participants designed action plans to address food safety at the Colon Night Market. Some Movers want to address the lack of housing for displaced families in Minglanilla. One Mover hoped to champion the rights of people with dwarfism.

Meanwhile, Movers who wanted to specialize in community journalism pitched stories tackling gut issues in Cebu, like substandard flood control projects, child labor, and how neighborhood carinderias navigate inflation to keep meals affordable.

Our civil society and academe partners matched this energy during our Partners’ Huddle, where they decided to prioritize four crisis clusters: Ecological, Governance, Services, and Displacement. Together, partners committed to lobbying local councils to prioritize environmental policy over profit, conducting citizen audits, raising awareness of and tackling the energy crisis plaguing Cebu, and fighting for humane relocation sites and protected municipal waters for fishing communities.

Movers and partners are already coordinating on next steps in the Padayon Cebu chat room on the Muni app. To be part of the action, you can join the chat room by downloading the Rappler app for free. If you would like to support Rappler’s Cebu coverage, we hope you consider becoming a Rappler+ member. Rappler+ is our premium membership program that allows you to experience the best of our journalism, while supporting our work. You can join Rappler+ here. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Over 141,000 personnel to be deployed for Undas 2026
articles.summary: More than 141,000 personnel from the Philippine National Police (PNP) and partner agencies will be deployed nationwide for security and public safety operations during Undas 2026.

blocks.text: More than 141,000 personnel from the Philippine National Police (PNP) and partner agencies will be deployed nationwide for security and public safety operations during Undas 2026.

“A grand total of 141,172. This comprises our PNP personnel, other units, yung mga partner agencies natin, like [Armed Forces of the Philippines], [Bureau of Fire Protections], [Philippuine Coast Guard], and of course, yung force multipliers po natin mga tanod and other [non-government organizations]," PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said at a press briefing.

(A grand total of 141,172. This comprises our PNP personnel, other units, our partner agencies, like Armed Forces of the Philippines, Bureau of Fire Protections, Philippine Coast Guard, and of course, our force multipliers.)

The deployment aims to help ensure public safety and maintain peace and order as Filipinos travel to their home provinces and visit cemeteries during the observance of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day on November 1 and 2.
The PNP said it would deploy personnel at transportation hubs, including airports, seaports and bus terminals amid expectations of increased passenger traffic.
Authorities expect travel activity to increase on the evening of October 29, with a more significant increase anticipated on the afternoon of October 30.
The police are also preparing traffic advisories covering road closures and alternative routes to guide motorists and commuters. These will be released once finalized, the PNP said.
Co said it would adjust deployment plans based on expected travel patterns, the calendar and security requirements.

The PNP will remain on full alert through November 2, with the status scheduled for possible downgrading or lifting on November 3, depending on the prevailing situation and the need for continued heightened security. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Arab parties could hold key as Netanyahu and Eisenkot set to fall short of victory
articles.summary: The two main blocs appear to have too few seats to form the next government without reliance on Arab parties.

blocks.text: With results still trickling in, it currently appears that Israel's veteran Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done better than was widely predicted with his Likud emerging as the largest single party.

His existing bloc with ultra-nationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties appear to be just short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. However, analysts caution that this is subject to change because the early count was skewed towards areas known to have strong right-wing support.
A dramatic deadlock had been widely forecast as Israelis surged to the polls – with turnout reaching more than 77%.

In Israel's fragmented political system, the signs are that Netanyahu's main rival, the former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, would struggle to command a parliamentary majority without parties led by Israel's Arab minority. According to partial results, they have equalled or gained on their previous record number of seats.
On the campaign trail, most Jewish opposition parties pledged not to work with Arab-majority lists, citing a lack of shared values.

However, Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if others were prepared to join forces with them. In this election, Arab Israelis – who often identify as Palestinian citizens of Israel and represent one-fifth of the population – appeared to turn out in unprecedented numbers.
Many saw this as a make-or-break election to defeat Israel's most right-wing-ever government, accusing it of stoking racism and hatred.

A huge caveat in all of the current analysis is that the high number of as-yet-uncounted absentee ballots – mostly representing the votes of Israeli soldiers – mean that we are not expecting to have a clear idea of the final results for another day or two.
Overnight, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot addressed their supporters, pledging to form the next government.

"The right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public, among the Jewish public and all those who support the Jewish state. That is what has become clear. A decisive majority," the PM told his celebrating supporters – although he stopped short of declaring victory.
"We must form a strong, national, right-wing government. That is what must be done," he added.

"The public has chosen change," Eisenkot told his Yashar party after exit polls came out – most of which were initially more favourable to the opposition. "The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust. The Israeli public voted against Benjamin Netanyahu continuing as prime minister."

"I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israeli's citizens. And quickly – because that is what this moment demands, and because the country needs to be brought back together."

There are deep divisions in Israeli society which have been underscored by this and previous elections. They have served not just as referenda on Netanyahu's leadership – as he faces a corruption trial on charges he denies – but also as votes on what kind of country Israel should be.

The PM and his current coalition partners have taken the country on a hardline religious, nationalist trajectory over the past four years. There were mass protests over their plan for a judicial overhaul prior to the unprecedented Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023 which triggered a series of wars – in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Many Israelis want to see their country more firmly anchored in liberal and secular values.
Remarkably, the past four turbulent years do not appear to have significantly changed voting patterns.

"We see in the polls, that the relative weight of the two main sides: pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu is about the same," Professor Tamar Hermann, a pollster at the Israeli Democracy Institute told me, just prior to the election. "People expected that after October 7th, Netanyahu will be down the drain or even toppled but it didn't happen."
Already, overnight, the main Israeli parties will have begun their intense political wrangling to try to form a new coalition government.

"Each side will try to pull over defectors, or will try to see if they can make a minority government and will try all these different political kinds of wizardry," is how veteran Israeli journalist and author, Yaakov Katz described the process to me. "But it might not work, and it could take weeks or months to see if someone is actually capable of forming a government."
The leaders of the bigger parties typically try to win over smaller ones with promises of cabinet positions, budgets or specific policies.
It is key now to see if those in the main opposition "change bloc" are ready to break a taboo by seeking a political deal with the Arab parties.

On the campaign trail, one of the bloc's leaders, right-wing politician Avigdor Lieberman, went as far as to say that he would not sit in a minority government that relied on their support. It was a sign of the increased mistrust and hostility towards Arab citizens since the 7 October assault.

When I recently met Mansour Abbas, head of Ra'am – the smaller of the two Arab lists – he told me that having been part of the diverse coalition that temporarily unseated Netanyahu between 2021 and 2022, he wanted to join the next government. He believed that potential partners would be more open to an alliance after the election.

"These are familiar and well-known party-political considerations. All politicians in Israel say one thing before elections and speak a different language after elections," he said. "We have experienced this before, and it does not concern us."
Meanwhile, Netanyahu and his allies have already begun an intense campaign of delegitimising the Arab parties – casting their fellow citizens as a threat from within.
So what are the next steps?

After the final results are presented to Israel's largely ceremonial president, Isaac Herzog, next week, he will consult all the leaders of elected parties and ask the candidate who appears most likely to form a coalition to do so.
If that candidate is unable to pull together a majority within a maximum of six weeks, then others could be allowed to try.
If, after all the haggling, no-one is able to form a governing coalition, a new election will be held in the following months, and the entire process will be repeated.
In the meantime, Netanyahu's government stays on in a caretaker role but without the authority to enact major policy changes.

articles.title: PH spotlights South China Sea, ‘fragmenting world’ in ASEAN defense chiefs’ meeting
articles.summary: Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun skips the ADMM-Plus meeting, as bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing hit their tensest note yet

blocks.text: Philippines Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro delivers opening remarks during the 20th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) at the Mactan Expo in Cebu, Philippines 28 October 2026.
Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun skips the ADMM-Plus meeting, as bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing hit their tensest note yet

items: Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. emphasized the importance of unity among ASEAN members despite differing ties with China, advocating for peaceful resolution of disputes, particularly in the South China Sea.

The ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting in Cebu will address regional security, disaster risk reduction, and cooperation on critical infrastructure, food, and energy security, with participation from defense ministers of Southeast Asia and dialogue partners.

Teodoro's leadership comes amid tense PH-China relations, with the Philippines strengthening defense ties with the US and Japan, while navigating the complexities of ASEAN's diverse relationships with China.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CEBU, Philippines — Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. told Southeast Asian defense chiefs, whose countries have widely varying ties with superpower China, that the bloc should “not allow differences to divide us from within.”

“ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] was founded on the belief that our strength lies in our diversity. We must therefore not allow our differences to divide us from within, and where such differences exist, including in the South China Sea, we shall settle them through peaceful and legal means,” said Teodoro, chairman of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting, to open the event on Wednesday, October 28.

Regional security, as well as bloc cooperation over issues like disaster risk reduction, will be among the key issues defense officials are expected to tackle in meetings and sideline events from October 28 to 29 at the Mactan Expo in Lapu-Lapu City.

Ministers, as well as working groups, are also expected to tackle protection of underwater critical infrastructure, cooperation for food and energy security, and preparedness for the super El Niño and its possible effects on security.

blocks.caption: PH spotlights South China Sea, ‘fragmenting world’ in ASEAN defense chiefs’ meeting

blocks.text: ADMM and the ADMM-Plus is an annual gathering of defense ministers from Southeast Asia and “plus countries” or ADMM dialogue partners Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States. It is the largest defense diplomacy gathering in ASEAN for the calendar year.

Aside from all 11 defense chiefs from Southeast Asia, their counterparts for almost all plus countries, including US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Japan Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro, are participating in the meetings.

blocks.caption: Hegseth likely to face questions on US role in Indo-Pacific at ASEAN summit in Cebu

blocks.text: As chair of ADMM, Teodoro will preside over all meetings, including two separate “informal meetings” with the US and Japan.
China’s Dong Jun will not be attending ADMM+. Beijing will instead be represented by its defense attache assigned to the Chinese embassy in Manila.
Cebu province has hosted several meetings under the Philippines’ chairmanship, including the first Foreign Ministers’ meeting, and the Summit in May.

“In a fragmenting world, our internal stability and intra-ASEAN unity are vital, perhaps even, in the future, existential. For it is only when we are united that we can effectively uphold ASEAN centrality and the principles that bind us, such as mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, peaceful settlement of disputes, and the renunciation of the threat or use of force,” said Teodoro, in remarks that preceded a direct mention of the South China Sea.
While disputes over and tensions in the critical waterway won’t be the center of discussions in Cebu, they certainly backdrop the Philippines’ chairmanship both of ASEAN and ADMM.

Teodoro, among the loudest critics of Beijing in the Philippine government, is barred from entering and transacting in China over his statements against the Asian superpower. Just weeks before ADMM, China’s ambassador to Manila was criticized for saying the Philippines should be thankful that they do not use force in its disputes — a statement made in reaction to Teodoro’s assertion that it was Beijing who was causing trouble in the region.

China claims almost all of the South China Sea, based on a supposed historical claim that a landmark 2016 Arbitral Award deemed invalid. Their claim overlaps with maritime claims and entitlements of several ASEAN members, including the Philippines.

In the West Philippine Sea, an area that includes the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, those overlapping claims have meant recurring confrontations between Chinese and Philippine maritime forces in some areas and features.
Tensions in the South China Sea is a concern for ASEAN not only because several members are claimants. The waterway is where up to a third of global trade passes through.

“ASEAN was founded on the belief that our strength lies in our diversity. We must therefore not allow our differences to divide us from within, and where such differences exist, including in the South China Sea, we shall settle them through peaceful and legal means,” said Teodoro.

blocks.caption: ADMM CHAIR. Philippines’ Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. waits for his counterparts’ arrival during the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM), Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, in Cebu, central Philippines.

blocks.text: As chair of ADMM, it’s the Philippines who steers the agenda. It’s almost no surprise that in Cebu, the Philippines is hosting two “informal meetings” with treaty-ally United States and close partner Japan.

Manila’s defense and security ties are deepest and most developed with Washington DC and Tokyo. The two countries are its staunchest partners in South China Sea issues and in its push to modernize the Philippine military. Manila is the first recipient of Japan’s Official Security Assistance (OSA). The US has allocated over $2.5 billion over five years in foreign military financing for the Philippines.

Teodoro is also expected to host a quadrilateral meeting between Hegseth, Koizumi, and Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles, a grouping known colloquially as the SQUAD.
The Philippines’ defense engagements — both with traditional and new partners — is spurred, in no small way, by maritime tensions with China.

In ASEAN, member states have varying degrees of closeness and cooperation with Beijing. It’s a difference that’s made cohesion a challenge, especially in a bloc that puts centrality and unanimity at the center of its decision-making and policy-making process. – Rappler.com
